# factory-repo

An experiment in running [CodeAF](https://github.com/Agent-Field/CodeAF) entirely inside
GitHub: issues go in, CodeAF does the work in GitHub Actions, and pull requests come out.

It is set up as a monorepo:
- applications live under `app/<name>/`, each its own Go module with its own README
  and licence;
- CI checks every module separately;
- the first application here is [kube-sqlite3-vfs](app/kube-sqlite3-vfs/README.md), a SQLite VFS that stores database files in Kubernetes ConfigMaps;
- the CodeAF harness and CI live in `.github/`.

## Using it

| You do | CodeAF does |
|---|---|
| Add the **`codeaf`** label to an issue | Works the issue on a new branch `codeaf/issue-N-<run id>` cut from the default branch and opens its own PR (labelled `codeaf`), so re-running never collides with an earlier run |
| Comment `/codeaf <instructions>` on a `codeaf`-labelled PR | Continues on the PR's branch with your instructions, the review comments and the conversation |
| Submit a **Request changes** review on a `codeaf`-labelled PR | Same as above, using the review as the instructions |
| Comment `/codeaf <instructions>` on a `codeaf`-labelled issue | Re-runs the issue on a new branch and opens a new PR; earlier runs' branches and PRs are left alone |

Nothing else triggers it. Only people with triage access can add labels, and `/codeaf`
commands are obeyed only from repository owners, members and collaborators, so
outside contributors cannot spend the API budget. PRs from forks are ignored.

Every run posts a report comment with CodeAF's outcome, a per-model cost table —
including each model's reasoning share (exact from reasoning tokens, or an estimate
labeled “(chars)” from character counts when the model does not report them) — and the
run's timing figures (wall time, time with a call in flight, tokens/s, longest call).
Three workflow artifacts are uploaded, none of them encrypted:
- `codeaf-output-*` (14 days): the patch, its base commit, CodeAF's JSON result
  and the call ledger (each call's start and duration, slot wait, reasoning tokens,
  and the reasoning/output character counts backing the estimate);
- `codeaf-diagnostics-*` (30 days): the brief, CodeAF's stderr, its run records
  (prompts, replies, tool output), call log and usage, and the proxy log;
- `codeaf-state-*` (14 days): what the run left in CodeAF's home, and what it
  cost, for the shared state below.

### Independent review of every PR (issue #32)

Every CodeAF run that opens or updates a pull request is followed by one
**review run** — a second CodeAF run in read-only review mode. The reviewer
sits on a different model from the worker that wrote the patch (worker
**GLM-5.3-Flash**, reviewer **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash**, both from
[`models.json`](.github/codeaf/models.json)), so it does not share the same
blind spots. It reviews the PR's diff against the issue for correctness,
concurrency, error handling and whether the tests actually exercise the
claims, and it re-runs the benchmarks the patch claims.

It posts one findings comment on the PR, with a severity and a file:line for
each finding. When anything is high or medium, that comment doubles as a
`/codeaf fix` command and a fix run starts on the PR's branch, counted
against the same continuation cap as the auto-continue feature — **2 per PR**.
When nothing blocks, the PR gets the **`codeaf-review-passed`** label, so a
person or a merge rule can merge with confidence.

The review run never publishes anything: it has no write token, and `publish`
applies no patch from it. Starting it goes through the same gate, spend caps
and state merge as any other run. The workflow change itself needs a
maintainer's approval, like any other change under `.github/`.

## How it is wired

- [`.github/workflows/codeaf.yml`](.github/workflows/codeaf.yml) runs three jobs,
  each checked out at the default branch:
  - `gate` checks the event against the rules above (`harness gate`).
  - `run`, which has no write token, builds CodeAF at the commit pinned in
    [`codeaf-ref`](.github/codeaf/codeaf-ref), writes a brief from the
    issue/PR, runs `codeaf do` headless and hands over a patch. The agent
    runs as its own unprivileged user -- created fresh each run with no
    sudo, handed the working tree and CodeAF's home for the run, started in
    a session of its own -- so it can neither signal nor read the runner
    (`Runner.Worker`, the pricing proxy) or use the runner's sudo; the
    workflow proves that with probes before the agent starts.
  - `publish`, on a fresh runner, checks and applies the patch, then commits,
    pushes, opens or updates the PR and dispatches [CI](.github/workflows/ci.yml).
    Pushes made with `GITHUB_TOKEN` do not trigger CI on their own.
- [`.github/codeaf/main.go`](.github/codeaf/main.go) is the harness: a standalone,
  standard-library-only Go program, with tests, that the workflow builds on every run.
  It decides whether an event may run (`gate`), writes the brief (`brief`), and renders
  the cost report (`report`). As `harness proxy` it runs on `127.0.0.1` for the
  length of the job and sits between CodeAF and [synthetic.new](https://synthetic.new).
  It:
  - serves CodeAF an OpenRouter-style `/models` catalog containing only the models in
    [`models.json`](.github/codeaf/models.json), at synthetic.new's **subscription
    rates** — the prices that draw down the weekly credit, so CodeAF's estimates and
    model routing see what usage really costs against the quota; the same file also
    carries each model's API list rates (`api_*`), what overage past the quota costs
    (both checked 2026-10-17, [synthetic.new/pricing](https://synthetic.new/pricing));
  - adds `usage.cost` to every response, which is where CodeAF's spend accounting
    reads cost from;
  - refuses any other model, and returns HTTP 402 once the run reaches its per-run
    credit cap (**$5**, `limits.run_credit_usd`) or the week's credit is gone
    (`limits.weekly_credit_usd`, from the shared state); with `overage_usd` 0 (the
    default) it stops there rather than pay API prices;
  - asks synthetic.new for the subscription state once at proxy start
    (`GET /v2/quotas` — the call does not count against the subscription's limits),
    logs the raw response into the diagnostics with no key, shows its fields in the
    report, and refuses a call early when the quota reports exhausted and overage is
    0. The response's units are undocumented, so the parse is defensive and an
    unfamiliar shape never fails a run;

  The synthetic.new key (`SYNTHETIC_API_KEY` secret) is held only by the proxy. It is
  passed in on stdin, not through the environment.
- Model choice: the seats are spread across models. synthetic.new used to
  allow only 2 calls to each model at once; since the October 2026 pricing
  change concurrency is by plan priority instead, and the factory sets its
  own per-model cap (`max_concurrent`, 8):
  - the worker runs on **GLM-5.3-Flash** ($0.10 in / $0.25 out per M tokens at
    subscription rates);
  - the planner and checker run on **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** ($0.06 / $0.30).
  - CodeAF's `task.parallel` is set per run to that run's slice of the
    worker model's `max_concurrent` (below).
  - The proxy enforces the limit per model (`max_concurrent` in
    `models.json`): a call past it waits for a slot instead of reaching
    synthetic.new. Each wait is written to the proxy log and the call
    ledger, so the diagnostics show whether a run was held up by it.
  - Escalation is switched off for now. CodeAF's cascade
    ([`panel.json`](.github/codeaf/panel.json)) would escalate to
    **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** ($0.06 / $0.30) and then **GLM-5.3** ($0.40 / $2.20),
    but it has two bugs:
    - it treats a reply made only of tool calls as empty, and fails every run;
    - its pinned rungs all call the seat model, so it never escalates.
  - [`codeaf.yml`](.github/workflows/codeaf.yml) explains how to turn it back on
    once CodeAF is fixed.

### Web search through the proxy (issue #58)

The proxy also serves CodeAF's web searches: `POST /v2/search` on `127.0.0.1`,
forwarded to [synthetic.new's search API](https://dev.synthetic.new/docs/synthetic/search).
CodeAF calls it with `harness search "<query>" [--limit N]` (the `harness`
binary is on the agent's `PATH`) and gets plain text back — numbered blocks
with title, URL, published date and the result text, capped per result. The
request is validated before forwarding (a non-empty `query` of at most 1,000
characters; only `query` is forwarded) and the response is capped at 1 MiB.
The key stays inside the proxy, as above — CodeAF never sees it. The query
itself does leave the runner and reach synthetic.new (zero data retention per
its docs); the price is undocumented, so each search is recorded in the ledger
with kind `search` and cost 0 until it is priced, and the report shows a "web
searches" row when a run made any. `limits.searches_per_run` (50 in
[`models.json`](.github/codeaf/models.json)) caps the searches one run may
forward; past it the proxy answers HTTP 429. Search results are untrusted text
from the internet — data, not instructions (see
[`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md#web-search)).

### Billing model (Big plan, issue #59)

The synthetic.new account is on the **Big** plan ($90/mo). Usage draws down a
**weekly credit** at the subscription rates, and the credit regenerates 2% of its
total every 202 minutes (~3.4 h) — a full refill in about a week. Past the quota,
usage is billed at the **API list prices**, up to `limits.overage_usd`; at 0 (the
default) the factory stops rather than pay beyond the $90. The Big plan's weekly
credit is not published, so `weekly_credit_usd` (22, an estimate from `/v2/quotas`) is a conservative
**assumption** — calibrate it from `GET /v2/quotas`'s `subscription.limit` once
its units are known. `run_credit_usd` (5) caps one run; the weekly credit and the
overage cap are shared by every run of the week through the shared state, and are
sized so several overlapping runs (`task.parallel` 2) can share the week.

What the harness does with it:
- the catalog prices CodeAF sees are the subscription rates — the credit;
  `api_input`/`api_cached`/`api_output` in the same file price the overage;
- the shared state carries the rolling 7-day credit spend; `harness state load`
  outputs the day's and the week's figure, and the queue starts a run only while the
  rolling week is under 75% of the weekly credit (`CODEAF_WEEK_SPENT_USD` — an
  unknown spend starts nothing);
- the proxy refuses at the weekly credit unless `overage_usd` > 0, and prices
  past-quota calls at the API rates against the overage cap;
- at proxy start it calls `GET /v2/quotas` (the call does not count against the
  subscription's limits), logs the raw body into the diagnostics with no key, shows
  it in the report, and refuses when the quota reports exhausted and overage is 0;
  the parse is defensive — unfamiliar fields never fail a run.

CodeAF's own config maps onto this as closely as its settings allow: CodeAF has no
weekly-budget key, and `daily_budget_usd`'s window is a single run's lifetime, so
it is set to 20 (the weekly credit, the closest match) with `models.crew.cap` 20;
`task_cap` 5 matches `run_credit_usd`.

**Fast and Infinite modes (beta) — follow-up only, nothing enabled.** Fast mode is
not enabled on the account and is not requested: the goal is more tickets, not
faster ones. Infinite mode is a proposed follow-up: its requests never count against
the rate limit, run outside the quota but much slower, and are DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
only — a way to add review/planner capacity without using the weekly credit. A
request opts in per request: per the API docs (checked 2026-10-17,
[dev.synthetic.new/docs/api/models](https://dev.synthetic.new/docs/api/models)), by
sending the model as the `infinite:` alias (`infinite:small:vision` resolves to
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), which requires `stream: true` and a Big plan. The `:flex`
model suffix suggested in the issue is not documented anywhere reachable.

## The queue

Issues labelled **`codeaf-queued`** are the backlog. Every 10 minutes (and on
demand, via *Run workflow*)
[`codeaf-queue.yml`](.github/workflows/codeaf-queue.yml) asks the harness
(`harness next`) to start the next run: the oldest queued issue —
**`codeaf-priority`** jumps the queue — for which all of these hold:

- fewer than `queue.max_parallel_runs` (in
  [`models.json`](.github/codeaf/models.json), default 2) `codeaf.yml` runs
  are queued or in progress — issue runs, PR continuations and review runs
  alike;
- no area conflict with an in-flight run: areas are `app/<name>/` per app
  and the harness `.github/`, taken from `area:` labels or paths in the
  issue body; an issue with no area conflicts with everything;
- every issue named in a "Depends on #N" line in its body is closed;
- the rolling week's credit spend in the shared state is under 75% of
  `limits.weekly_credit_usd` in [`models.json`](.github/codeaf/models.json) — an
  unknown spend starts nothing;
- the issue is queued and not already active.

A run is started by adding the **`codeaf`** label — the same trust gate as a
person adding it — and then by dispatching
[`codeaf.yml`](.github/workflows/codeaf.yml) with the issue number. The
dispatch step exists because events raised with `GITHUB_TOKEN` (labelling
included) do not trigger other workflows; `workflow_dispatch` is the one event
it can start. The queue starts runs only up to the parallel-run limit, and
never two on the same area, so queued work overlaps only where those rules
allow ([running several tickets at once](#running-several-tickets-at-once-issue-60)).
Runs started by hand (a label or a `/codeaf` comment) can still overlap with
them; they are not held in a single
concurrency group, because GitHub would cancel all but the newest pending run
in it and silently drop a command.

Manual controls: *Run workflow* on either workflow — `codeaf-queue.yml` runs
the queue's checks now, `codeaf.yml` starts an issue when given its number.
Known failure modes:
- a "Depends on #N" line naming an open pull request blocks too (the issues
  API lists PRs);
- if the dispatch step fails after labelling, the issue keeps `codeaf` but
  nothing runs — a maintainer runs `codeaf.yml` by hand with the issue number;
- a self-dependency or a dependency cycle blocks the issue until its body is
  edited;
- two queue ticks in quick succession can miss a just-dispatched run in the
  runs list, and the runs then share lane 0 — the per-model per-run slots
  keep the account limit safe regardless.

### Running several tickets at once (issue #60)

The queue starts up to **`queue.max_parallel_runs`** runs at once (in
[`models.json`](.github/codeaf/models.json), default 2). Everything
`codeaf.yml` runs counts toward that limit while it is queued or in
progress: issue runs, continuations of runs that stopped early, and review
runs alike.

**Lanes.** Each run the queue starts gets the lowest free lane, 0 through
`max_parallel_runs - 1`. The lane picks the run's worker seat model from the
allowed list in `models.json`, as `models[lane mod count]`, so two
concurrent runs rarely compete for one model's call slots; lane 0 keeps
today's default seat, GLM-5.3-Flash. The lane travels to the run as a
digits-only `workflow_dispatch` input, validated by the gate and validated
again by `seat-config` inside the run job — a missing or malformed lane
means lane 0. The queue reads lanes back from run titles, which read
`CodeAF #N (lane L)`; titles are untrusted data, and a title that does not
parse counts as lane 0.

**The per-model cap is account-wide.** `max_concurrent` is meant for the
whole account, and every run has its own proxy, so without slicing four runs
could each put the full cap on one model. Instead each run gets a
slice of every model's `max_concurrent`: per-run slots =
`max_concurrent / max_parallel_runs`, at least 1, with CodeAF's
`task.parallel` set to match. The proxy enforces the slice, and `loadConfig`
refuses a `max_parallel_runs` that would overflow a model, so runs sharing
one model never sum past `max_concurrent` (8 per model, at 4 runs: 2 each). Manual runs (a label or a
`/codeaf` comment) carry no lane and still overlap without coordination; the
slice caps them at 2 calls per model per run.

**Area conflicts.** The queue does not start a run on an area another run is
already working. Areas are `app/<name>/` for each app and the harness
(`.github/`), taken from `area:harness` and `area:app/<name>` labels or from
paths in the issue body. An issue with no area conflicts with everything,
and so does an in-flight run whose area is unknown.

**The budget.** Unchanged: the queue holds new starts once the shared
rolling-week spend reaches 75% of `limits.weekly_credit_usd`, and all
concurrent runs draw that budget down together.

**Pricing.** At the subscription rates, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash has the cheapest
input price (0.06 USD/M tokens), so a non-zero lane can spend less credit
per ticket — but it is a weaker model (`role: mid`), so the rotation trades
a little quality on busy days for no model contention.

**Where to see it.** The queue job's log lists the runs in progress, the
lanes in use, and why each candidate started or was held.

### Model experiments

To tell what is down to the model from what is down to the harness, the
same task can be run with different seat models. An experiment issue carries
the `codeaf-experiment` label and runs only when dispatched with a `profile`
input naming one of the profiles in `.github/codeaf/experiments.json`:

```sh
gh workflow run codeaf.yml -f issue=N -f lane=0 -f profile=kimi
```

A profile pins the worker, planner and checker seats to models from
`models.json`; the gate and `seat-config` both validate the name. Labels and
`/codeaf` comments never start an experiment issue, and a profile on any
other issue is refused. A profile run gets no independent review and no
continuation, so each result is that profile's unaided work. Models with
role `experiment` (Kimi-K3) are allowed by the proxy but never picked as a
lane's worker.

### Runs that stop early (issue #31)

A run can stop before it is finished: CodeAF reports `stop: deadline` (it used
its 100 minutes), `incomplete`, or a budget stop — the per-run credit cap, or the
weekly credit with `overage_usd` 0, in [`models.json`](.github/codeaf/models.json).
The patch is still published, as a
**draft** pull request whose body says the run stopped early, why, and that the
work is unverified: after the push, `publish` asks the harness
([`main.go`](.github/codeaf/main.go), `harness pr-mode`) how the run ended.

For a stop a continuation can help (`deadline`, `incomplete` and the budget
family; other stops, an `error` say, leave the draft to a person), the workflow
then posts `/codeaf continue: <reason>` on that PR and dispatches
[`codeaf.yml`](.github/workflows/codeaf.yml) with its new `pr` input, which
starts a run on the PR's branch. The continuation's brief carries the previous
run's report and what the issue the PR closes still requires. The chain is
capped at **2 continuations per issue**, counted from the PR's own CodeAF
report comments — the first report is the run that opened the PR, not a
continuation. At the cap the PR gets a comment and stays a draft for a person
(a maintainer can still continue it by hand with a `/codeaf` comment). A run
that ends with `stop: done` marks the PR ready for review.

### Bringing the base branch in (issue #57)

A pull request that conflicts with the default branch used to stay dirty
forever. The run job hands `publish` a patch against the PR branch's head,
`publish` applies it and pushes a plain commit, and nothing ever made a
merge commit -- so the branch never contained `main`, and a person had to
resolve the conflict by hand. In PR mode the run job now merges the PR base
branch's tip into the PR head **before** CodeAF works. A clean merge is
committed as an ordinary merge commit. A conflicting merge is committed
too, with the conflict markers left in the files: the run's base commit
becomes that merge commit, and the brief names the conflicted files and
tells CodeAF to remove every conflict marker (the lines starting with
`<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>`). The merge commit exists only in the
run job's checkout -- the run has no write token and never pushes.

`publish`, which treats everything from `run` as untrusted data, recreates
the merge commit itself from the same two parents (the PR head and the
base tip) and refuses unless the tree hash it computes matches the tree
recorded in the run's `merge-info.json` artifact (its fields: a kind of
`clean` or `conflicted`, commit, base, onto, tree, files). It then applies
the patch -- the patch is what removes the markers -- and refuses the
whole publish if any conflict marker is left in the previously conflicted
files. When there is no `merge-info.json` (the run died before merging,
say), `publish` keeps a fallback: it merges the base tip first, then
applies the patch. The invariants do not move: `git apply` is still the
only thing applied from `run`, the `.github/` approval check still applies
to the staged patch diff only, and every new commit still descends from
the PR head -- no force-push.

One limit: if the base branch changed anything under `.github/workflows/`
since the PR branched, the base is **not** brought in, by the run job or by
`publish`. GitHub refuses a `GITHUB_TOKEN` push that carries workflow
changes, so the patch is pushed alone, as before, and the PR stays behind
its base until a maintainer updates the branch.

### Keeping CodeAF current (issue #35)

The CodeAF version is pinned by a full commit SHA in
[`codeaf-ref`](.github/codeaf/codeaf-ref), a config file under `.github/codeaf/`
rather than a workflow variable: [`codeaf.yml`](.github/workflows/codeaf.yml)
reads it from the default-branch checkout and refuses to run if the file is
missing or not exactly 40 hex characters. A bump is now a one-line change to
that file, which publishes like app code and needs no maintainer approval —
unlike the old hardcoded `CODEAF_REF` env in the workflow, which made every
bump a workflow edit that needs one.

Every Monday morning [`codeaf-ref-check.yml`](.github/workflows/codeaf-ref-check.yml)
(scheduled, and on demand via *Run workflow*) compares the pin with upstream
`Agent-Field/codeaf` `main` (`harness ref-check`). When upstream has moved, it
opens — or updates, if one exists — **one** issue, labelled
**`codeaf-ref-update`** and **`codeaf-queued`** for the queue, listing the
upstream commits since the pin and asking CodeAF to say which of the
workarounds documented in this README they make unnecessary, and to bump the
pin and remove those workarounds only if a test run on a small task succeeds.
When the pin has caught up, the check closes the issue again.

A bump can also be done by hand: edit the pin file to the new full commit SHA.
Removing workflow-level workarounds is a workflow change and still needs a
maintainer's approval (the `codeaf-harness` environment, see
*Limits worth knowing* below).

## Limits worth knowing

- The agent has a shell on the runner, so treat it as having the same access as any
  CI job. It gets no GitHub token: the checkout does not keep credentials, and the
  workflow pushes after CodeAF exits.
- CodeAF may change `.github/` (the harness, CI and workflows) when a task asks
  for it.
  - A change only to `.github/codeaf/` (the harness program, `models.json`,
    `codeaf-config.json`) is published like app code. Every job that holds a
    secret or a write token builds the harness from `main`, so the change
    takes effect only once merged.
  - Any other change under `.github/` (workflows, `CODEOWNERS`) controls what
    CI runs with secrets. For those, `publish` runs in the
    **`codeaf-harness`** environment and waits for a maintainer
  to approve it in the run's page (GitHub emails the reviewers) before anything
  is pushed. It also checks the approval through the API, so a misconfigured
  environment refuses the patch rather than publishing it.
  - **Workflow changes without a maintainer.** A patch whose only such
    changes are top-level workflow files is published anyway if it passes
    the deterministic workflow policy (`harness workflow-policy`). The
    policy lets the patched workflows do nothing the default branch's
    can't:
    - no new triggers, permissions or environments;
    - no new or edited steps that reference secrets;
    - no new or unpinned actions;
    - no new `github.event` interpolation;
    - no new or deleted workflow files.

    The PR is labelled `codeaf-workflow-change`. The independent review run,
    on another model with a workflow-security checklist, must pass it before
    it is merged, and it is never merged automatically. Anything the policy
    refuses, such as an edit to a step that holds a secret, still waits for a
    maintainer.

  One-off setup:
  - *Settings → Environments → New environment* `codeaf-harness`:
    - **Required reviewers**: yourself. Leave *Prevent self-review* off, since
      the run is started by you.
    - **Deployment branches**: `main` only.
  - Create a GitHub App to push approved harness patches, so they don't
    go out as you. `GITHUB_TOKEN` can't push changes to
    `.github/workflows/`, so without the app only changes elsewhere under
    `.github/` can be published.
    1. *Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App*, for
       example "factory-repo CodeAF harness".
       - Untick *Webhook → Active*.
       - Repository permissions: *Contents* read and write, *Workflows* read
         and write. Nothing else.
       - *Only on this account*.
    2. Install it on `RichardoC/factory-repo` only.
    3. Generate a private key, then add two secrets to the `codeaf-harness`
       environment:
       - `CODEAF_APP_ID`: the app's ID;
       - `CODEAF_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`: the whole `.pem` file.
    4. Delete the downloaded key file.

    After approval, `publish` uses the key to mint a token that lasts an hour,
    for this repository only, with just those two permissions. It pushes with
    that token, so the push shows as `<app name>[bot]`.
- CodeAF runs in a job with no write access (`run`). A separate job on a fresh
  runner (`publish`) checks and applies the resulting patch, then commits,
  pushes, opens the PR and posts the report. Nothing CodeAF could have tampered
  with is executed with a write token.
- **Shared state.** Every run starts from one shared bundle:
  - CodeAF's memory db, router events and model ratings;
  - the rolling 7-day credit spend — credit at subscription rates, from the runs
    merged so far. The weekly credit regenerates continuously (2% of the total every
    ~202 minutes), and this rolling sum is what stands in for the refill; `state
    load` outputs both the day's and the week's figure.

  [`codeaf-state.yml`](.github/workflows/codeaf-state.yml) is the only writer:
  - It merges each run's `codeaf-state-*` artifact into a new generation of
    the bundle, saved in the Actions cache as `codeaf-shared-v1-g<N>-…`. The
    last five generations are kept.
  - The CodeAF workflow's `handoff` job starts it as soon as CodeAF has
    finished. It runs one merge at a time, and each merge picks up every run
    not merged yet.
  - When runs overlap, spend is added and ratings and events are merged. The
    memory db comes only from a run that started from the latest generation.

  Everything is checked before it is merged, and again before CodeAF sees it
  (see [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md#caches-and-carried-state)). Saved memories reach
  CodeAF's prompts. So to reset the state, delete the `codeaf-shared-v1-*`
  caches (*Actions → Caches*); to roll back, delete only the newest ones.
- CodeAF itself is rebuilt from source on every run; nothing executable is
  carried between runs.
- **Diagnostics are public.** Artifacts on a public repo can be downloaded by
  any signed-in GitHub user, and the diagnostics are not encrypted. They hold
  the brief, prompts, model replies and tool output, so never put anything
  secret in an issue or in the `run` job. Token-shaped strings are redacted
  before upload, as a backstop. The `CODEAF_ARTIFACT_PUBLIC_KEY` and
  `CODEAF_ARTIFACT_PRIVATE_KEY` secrets are no longer used and can be deleted.
- The rules for future changes are in
  [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md#security-rules-for-changing-the-harness).
- Protecting `main`: [`CODEOWNERS`](.github/CODEOWNERS) makes @RichardoC the owner of
  everything. Pair it with a ruleset on `main` that requires a PR, a Code Owner review,
  approval of the most recent push, and the `CI / go` check. A `github-actions[bot]`
  approval then never counts, even with the setting below enabled. The workflow itself
  never approves or merges anything.
- Repository setting needed: *Settings → Actions → General → Allow GitHub Actions to
  create and approve pull requests* (for `gh pr create` with `GITHUB_TOKEN`).
- Configuration lives in files, not workflow variables:
  - [`models.json`](.github/codeaf/models.json): the spend caps (`limits`: the plan,
    the weekly credit, the per-run credit and the overage cap) and the allowed models
    with their prices (USD per million tokens: the `input`/`output`/`cache_read`
    subscription rates draw down the weekly credit, `api_input`/`api_cached`/`api_output`
    are the API list rates overage is billed at), how many calls
    each may have in flight (`max_concurrent`), and the reasoning efforts each
    model accepts (`efforts`; a request for an unlisted effort goes to the next
    one the model lists, `enabled: false` to its lowest, so nothing is sent raw
    that the model does not list — see *GLM reasoning effort* below);
  - [`panel.json`](.github/codeaf/panel.json): the escalation order (not used for
    now, see above);
  - [`codeaf-config.json`](.github/codeaf/codeaf-config.json): CodeAF's own settings
    (seat models, how many tasks run at once, budgets, telemetry and Model Pool
    off), installed as its profile config.

  Keep the three consistent when changing models. Put seats that run at the
  same time on different models, and keep `task.parallel` no higher than the
  worker model's `max_concurrent`. The only CodeAF setting left in
  the environment is the endpoint (`CODEAF_BASE_URL`), because CodeAF reads it from
  nowhere else. The panel path (`CODEAF_MODELS`) would be the second one.

### GLM reasoning effort (issue #24)

GLM returns empty answers at `low`, so a request for an unlisted effort goes to the next
one the model lists; `low` is never sent to GLM. Measured 2026-10-17 on a real multi-step Go edit-and-test task through the
live proxy, 3 repeats per case (results.md, issue #24): `medium` matched `high` on correctness
for both models, saving ~19.3% median completion tokens and ~17.8% median wall s on
glm-5.3-flash, ~35.9% and ~32.1% on glm-5.3. Both now send `low`/`minimal`/`medium` as
`medium`: glm-5.3 cleared the 20% threshold, and the owner chose `medium` for glm-5.3-flash
too, since about 72% of its output is reasoning (the report's reasoning-share column).

| model | effort | median completion tokens | median wall s | success |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| glm-5.3-flash | medium | 993 | 19.8 | 3/3 |
| glm-5.3-flash | high | 1231 | 24.1 | 3/3 |
| glm-5.3 | medium | 854 | 17.8 | 3/3 |
| glm-5.3 | high | 1332 | 26.3 | 3/3 |

### GLM reasoning share (issue #25)

synthetic.new never sends `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` for GLM, so its
reasoning-token column reads `—` and the exact reasoning share is unavailable. GLM does
stream its reasoning as `reasoning_content` (and returns it in the non-streamed `message`),
so the proxy counts those characters — plus the visible `content` and tool-call argument
characters — out of the chunk/response decode it already performs, records them in the
ledger as `reasoning_chars`/`output_chars`, and the report renders such models' reasoning
share as an estimate labeled “(chars)” (`reasoning ÷ (reasoning + visible output)`).
Models that do report reasoning tokens keep the exact token-based share. Character counts
are bytes, not runes; the proportion — not the absolute figure — is what the estimate uses.

# REA-Reconstruction-Companion ![REA Reconstruction Companion — Understand. Rebuild. Validate.](assets/discord-banner.png) **Understand existing software. Plan a reconstruction. Build and validate when requested.** An open-source, model-independent Agent Skill that works with [REA](https://github.com/morluto/rea). Turn reverse-engineering evidence into requirements, architecture, an implementation roadmap and testable results—at the scope you choose. [Get started](#install-with-an-ai-agent) · [Usage examples](#use) · [REA integration](#optional-rea-integration) · [Documentation](#source-and-development) · [Releases](https://github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion/releases) · [Support on Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/shadowswaps) | Your goal | What the companion helps produce | | --- | --- | | Understand an app before rebuilding | Evidence-backed behavior, requirements, unknowns and a staged roadmap. | | Build a similar tool now | Scoped implementation in testable increments, with validation and reported differences. | | Investigate a feature, function or format | A focused contract and representative acceptance cases. | | Improve an existing reconstruction | Measurements, targeted changes and revalidation of affected behavior. | **Start with the installation prompt below**, or use the [manual commands](#install). The portable core has no model SDK or paid API requirement. [Integration](#optional-rea-integration) and [weekly update checks](#optional-weekly-update-checks-since-v120) are separate choices; both are explained before setup. ## Install with an AI agent Give this prompt to an agent with local file and command access. It identifies your client and asks for your integration preference; you do not need to fill in any placeholders. ```text Install REA-Reconstruction-Companion from: https://github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion Read README.md and INSTALL.md, identify my AI client and its skills directory, and follow the documented installation workflow. Before making installation changes, explain the optional REA integration rule and ask me to choose: - Enable: relevant REA reconstruction requests also load the companion, sharing evidence, requirements, and validation work. - Skip: install the companion without changing REA; I can invoke it explicitly. This does not remove an integration rule already installed. Wait for my choice unless I have already provided it. Then install using that setting, preview changes with --dry-run, preserve existing work and backups, and verify with --check. Explain any missing prerequisites or access limitations. Report what was installed, where, and whether the integration was enabled. Do not claim success unless verified. Also explain the optional weekly update check (included since v1.2.0) and ask whether I want it enabled. Keep it off unless I choose it. This checks on skill use and still asks me before installing an update. Do not incur additional charges: use existing local tools and do not activate billing, paid services, metered APIs, or automatic paid usage. If a step could incur a charge and that cannot be ruled out, stop that step and explain a no-charge alternative. ``` You can include "Enable integration" or "Skip integration" with the prompt to choose upfront. The [integration explanation](#optional-rea-integration) describes its purpose and benefits. A chat-only assistant without local file and command access can guide you through installation but cannot perform it itself. Share the repository: [github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion](https://github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion). ## Use You can explicitly invoke `$rea-reconstruction-companion` in Codex or `/rea-reconstruction-companion` in Claude Code. With integration enabled, a relevant request to REA also instructs the agent to load the companion. Describe the software and the outcome you want in ordinary language. The companion uses available REA tools or supplied evidence, identifies gaps, and keeps the work at your requested scope. These examples are illustrations, not required prompts: paraphrases, casual wording, minor typos and follow-ups should work in context. Say what you want to understand or build; you do not need to name a mode or reproduce a template. Explicit corrections and exclusions take precedence, and a possible future rebuild does not request implementation now. **Understand and plan a future reconstruction.** Expect evidence-backed behavior and workflow requirements, known unknowns, and a staged roadmap before implementation: ```text Use REA and the companion to understand the desktop notes app I have open so I can plan a similar app later. Focus on creating, editing, searching, and saving notes. Link requirements to the evidence, separate observations from inferences, and list unanswered questions and a staged build roadmap. Stop after the specification and plan. ``` **Build a similar app now.** A build request authorizes implementation within the requested scope. Expect incremental code changes and validation against observed requirements, with gaps and differences reported: ```text Use REA and the companion to investigate the desktop notes app I have open and build a local web app with similar note creation, editing, search, and save behavior in this workspace. Start with one working workflow, then add the remaining features in testable increments. Validate against the evidence and report differences and anything you could not verify. ``` **Investigate one function or feature.** Expect a focused contract covering inputs, outputs, side effects, errors, and evidence gaps: ```text Use REA and the companion to investigate the CSV import feature in the app I have open. Trace how it handles headers, quoted fields, duplicate rows, and malformed input. Document inputs, outputs, side effects, error behavior, and representative acceptance cases, citing the evidence. Keep this to an investigation; do not implement changes. ``` The agent must report missing tools or evidence instead of claiming live analysis or complete equivalence. A build request does not authorize deployment, releases, installation changes, paid tools, or additional charges. Those actions require their own authority; the no-additional-charges constraint below still applies. ### Continue or optimize a scoped implementation > Continue implementing the app from this project's REA reconstruction specification. > Reimplement the decodeFrame function in this library and make it faster for large inputs. Recover its contract, then compare correctness and performance. ### Resume earlier work > Pick up from this checkpoint. Keep the same scope, retain the passing evidence that still applies, and work on the next unfinished part. Select the checkpoint or its path and identify any changed target or goal. The agent should read that record and the sources needed for the next step, check evidence applicability, and preserve historical results. Resuming a specification does not authorize building it. See [portable checkpoint guidance](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/references/checkpoints.md) and the [worked resume example](evals/resume/WALKTHROUGH.md). For a small question, expect a compact evidence-linked answer or contract with limits and a useful next action. A feature build adds implementation and acceptance results; it need not produce a whole-app blueprint. If a consequential target or outcome is unclear, expect one focused clarification. Host activation and instruction following vary: explicit invocation can help select the skill, but examples and installation do not guarantee every host/model will interpret every phrasing correctly. To see the workflow before trying a target, follow the [worked investigation](evals/reference/WALKTHROUGH.md), [reconstruction](evals/reference/reconstruction/README.md), or [resume](evals/resume/WALKTHROUGH.md) for your goal. These disclose answers and prior source exposure; they are teaching material, not prerequisites or evidence of a fresh agent trial. The [first-use review](evals/first-use.md) separates manual intent scenarios from executable checks. ## What it does - Identifies the requested subject, evidence carrier, and objective from natural language. No form or bracketed prompt variables are required. - Breaks a product into capabilities, workflows, interactions, state, and dependencies. - Defines requirements, contracts, expected behavior, and acceptance criteria linked to evidence. - Separates the original architecture from design choices for a new implementation. - Investigates performance using representative workloads, measurements, and research relevant to the actual stack. - Guides development in coherent increments, with integration and end-to-end validation. - Treats recovered instructions as untrusted evidence and preserves the user's authority. - Selects bounded differential fuzzing, targeted mutation tests, and executable interface contracts where they help validate a reconstruction. - Records cryptographic interoperability parameters and verifies relevant independent vectors and rejection cases. - Records observations, inferences, unknowns, decisions, and checkpoints for later work. ## How it works with REA REA supplies the reverse-engineering tools and evidence workflow. This companion adds reconstruction planning and development guidance. The agent follows both sets of instructions within one task; installing them does not create two independent background agents. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[User goal and target] --> B[Scope and questions] B --> C[REA evidence] C --> D[Requirements and design] D --> E[Implementation when requested] E --> F[Validation and measurements] D -->|Evidence gap| C F -->|Evidence gap| C ``` For the method and its sources, see the [skill instructions](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/SKILL.md) and [research basis](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/references/research-basis.md). ## Install Download and extract the ZIP from [Releases](https://github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion/releases), or clone this repository. Run commands from the extracted folder or repository root. On Windows, macOS, and Linux, the installer commands are the same. For automatic co-use, first install [REA for your client](https://github.com/morluto/rea#readme). Then choose a command: ```sh # Claude Code, with the optional integration node install.mjs --client claude-code --integration on # Codex, with the optional integration node install.mjs --client codex --integration on # Companion only; no changes to REA node install.mjs --client claude-code --integration off ``` Use `--dry-run` on any installation command to inspect the paths and changes without writing files. The `companionChanges` lists identify added, modified, and removed files relative to the companion directory, including local files that a replacement would move into the backup. Use the same command with `--check` afterward to verify the selected installation mode. A missing REA skill or ambiguous choice stops integrated installation before the companion is installed. Differently cased paths to the same REA file are treated as one candidate; genuinely separate installations still require an explicit selection. `claude_code`, as used by REA, is accepted as an alias for `claude-code` by the installer and updater. Plans, receipts and newly saved update settings use `claude-code`.
Client paths, custom profiles and advanced installation Default user locations: - Claude Code: `~/.claude/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/`, or `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/` when a custom configuration directory is set in the installer's environment. See [Claude Code's environment-variable documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars). REA lookup stays within that selected profile unless `--rea-skill` explicitly selects another location. - Codex: `~/.agents/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/`, or `$CODEX_HOME/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/` when `CODEX_HOME` is set. The installer also checks the older `~/.codex/skills/` location when locating REA. - Generic clients: specify their documented skills directory with `--skills-dir`. Override paths for an existing installation, a project-scoped skill, or another agent: ```sh node install.mjs --client generic --integration on --skills-dir "/path/to/skills" --rea-skill "/path/to/reverse-engineer-anything/SKILL.md" ``` `--skills-dir` accepts the parent skills directory; the installer creates `rea-reconstruction-companion` beneath it. It takes precedence over client defaults and environment variables. The REA path must identify the skill actually loaded by that client. An override disables broad automatic lookup. Paths with spaces should be quoted. If the installer runs outside the agent's environment, supply that agent's actual directory explicitly. Keep the downloaded package or checkout separate from the installation destination. The installer rejects overlapping source/destination directories and a REA file inside the companion destination, including existing paths that differ only by casing on a filesystem that treats them as the same location. The optional `agents/openai.yaml` adapter is installed only for Codex. The portable core and Claude Code installation do not depend on it. Refresh the host's skills or start a fresh session if the new skill is not visible.
## Optional REA integration Choose one during installation: | Choice | What the installer does | When it helps | | --- | --- | --- | | `--integration on` | Adds a marked instruction block to your selected REA `SKILL.md`. | When you want relevant REA reconstruction requests to load the companion without naming it separately. | | `--integration off` | Installs only the companion and leaves REA untouched. | When you prefer explicitly invoking the companion or managing your own routing rules. | The integration asks the agent to use the companion for understanding a target **for reconstruction**, planning a similar implementation, or rebuilding selected functionality. Its benefits are shared evidence, a consistent requirements-to-test trail, and focused returns to REA when design or testing exposes an unanswered question. Ordinary explanations, comparisons, and diagnostics stay narrow. This is an instruction-based integration. It does not override client policies, grant tool permissions, connect MCP servers, guarantee model compliance, or force parallel execution. Without the rule, invoking the companion still tells the agent to use REA. The rule supplies the reverse direction: relevant REA work also loads the companion. **REA skill refreshes can remove this rule.** In REA 6.5.0 (skill version 42), `rea doctor` requires byte-for-byte canonical skill files, so adding our block can produce `skill:identity` / `config_drift` with “Installed REA skill identity is stale” even when version and tool count match. This is a known cause, not a reason to ignore all stale or doctor diagnostics: other managed files or settings may also differ. The pinned [identity check](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/3b79af28e80785afce9f5998d8f03289402a1847/src/application/Doctor.ts) and [skill installer](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/3b79af28e80785afce9f5998d8f03289402a1847/src/application/SetupSkill.ts) show why `rea setup` restores canonical files and preserves edited originals in backups, removing the active companion block. An REA update that refreshes the skill can do the same; other upstream versions may differ. After `rea setup`, `rea update`, or another REA skill refresh, recheck the selected integration and, if needed, restore only its block using the matching verified companion package; see [verification and scoped recovery](INSTALL.md#verify-and-report). Do not restore an entire old REA backup over newer instructions. If routing disappeared, explicitly invoke the companion or run the manual check. The optional on-use warning cannot run if the companion/helper is never invoked. `off` means **do not manage REA**, not “remove a rule already installed.” To disable an earlier integration, remove only the block between `` and `` in the selected REA `SKILL.md`, including the markers. Keep the rest of REA intact. ## Requirements and compatibility The core skill is plain Markdown in the [Agent Skills format](https://agentskills.io/specification). It has no model SDK, paid API requirement, Python dependency, telemetry, or background service. ### No additional charges The skill forbids initiating actions that could add charges: purchases, subscriptions/trials, metered APIs or model calls, billable cloud/CI/storage/deployment, and indirect paid work. Existing local tools and supplied evidence come first. If an action's no-charge status cannot be established for the actual environment, the agent must skip it and explain a local alternative or limitation. An available tool or a free tier is not sufficient evidence. It does not automatically launch agents, evaluations, or scheduled jobs. This rule is an instruction, not a billing enforcement mechanism. An AI host may itself bill tokens or usage credits, and local execution consumes resources such as electricity. The skill cannot guarantee zero total cost or control another product's billing or model compliance. It must not enable extra paid usage or alter billing settings; use host/account spending controls for an absolute spending limit. No paid exception is part of this skill's workflow. | Component | Requirement | | --- | --- | | Skill workflow | A capable agent that can read the skill and its references; REA tools or supplied REA evidence for actual investigation. | | Included installer | Node.js 20 or newer. Uses only Node's standard library; no `npm install`, PyYAML, or network access. | | Optional update helper (v1.2.0+) | Existing Node.js 20+. Uses the standard library and opt-in public GitHub requests; no packages, tokens, model calls or scheduler. | | REA | Installed and configured separately for your client. REA and target-specific engines have their own requirements. | | Release building | Python 3.10+ standard library, for maintainers only. Not needed to install or use the skill. | Codex and Claude Code both support filesystem skills. Their discovery locations and invocation syntax differ; the installer handles those differences. Other agents can use the same core files through an explicit skills directory. Compatibility depends on the host's file/tool access, not just the model name. See the official [Codex skill documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills) and [Claude Code skill documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills). Hosted uploads and chat-only clients are different: an uploaded skill ZIP cannot generally edit a separate local REA installation. Supply both skills and evidence through that host's supported mechanisms, or use a local agent for installation and live analysis. No live-model compatibility certification is implied by the installer tests. ## Optional weekly update checks (since v1.2.0) Starting with **v1.2.0**, the updater is bundled inside the skill, including installations for Codex, Claude Code and generic clients. Enable it once after installation if you want release notifications. The host calls a small local helper when the skill is used; it contacts GitHub only when seven days have elapsed. An idle skill runs nothing. Earlier versions do not gain this automatically: manually install a published v1.2.0-or-later package first. With checks enabled and recorded integration on, the current helper also inspects the recorded REA rule locally before cooldown or network decisions. Missing, changed/malformed, or unreadable/unsafe rules return `integration-needs-attention` without repair, state changes or networking. Disabled checks and integration off do not inspect REA. This warning is available only in versions containing this change and only when the companion/helper is invoked; it is not a background monitor or a full `rea doctor` check. When a newer stable release is found, the agent offers **Update now / Remind me next week / Skip this version / Disable checks**. No answer means no update. Approval is tied to the offered release and asset; changed assets require a new offer. Local customizations stop automatic replacement. Successful updates retain backups, verify the result and preserve your selected client and REA integration setting. Checks are **off by default**, independent of integration, and require existing Node.js 20+. There is no npm dependency, model/API key, paid service, extra model call, background daemon or scheduled AI task. Online operations also require confirmation that the actual network/tool environment cannot add charges. Unknown-cost or unavailable access is skipped; this is not an unconditional zero-resource-cost or billing-enforcement guarantee. Read the [setup, commands, state location and recovery guide](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/references/updates.md). Host instruction-following and local command access are required; the helper cannot force every AI host to invoke it or authenticate a human response. Installation refresh behavior depends on the host. The project owner's release approval process remains unchanged. ## Updates, backups, and recovery - Repeating the same installation is safe and does not duplicate the integration block. - Differing companion files require `--replace`; the installer backs up the entire prior companion directory before replacing it. - REA edits preserve everything outside the marked integration block. The exact earlier pre-release rule can also be migrated; customized unmarked rules require review. - Backups and a receipt are stored in `.rea-reconstruction-companion-installer/` next to the parent skills directory. The installer prints the exact transaction path. - Failed commits attempt REA and companion recovery independently, so an unreadable or missing REA file does not prevent restoring the prior companion. Backups remain available; a detected concurrent edit is retained and reported rather than overwritten. - Updating REA may replace its skill instructions. Follow [verification and scoped recovery](INSTALL.md#verify-and-report) after a refresh. Nothing monitors or rewrites REA in the background. For manual recovery, use the printed receipt to locate the selected paths. Restore `companion-before` to the companion's former location if appropriate. Restore `rea-before.md` only when REA has no later changes you need to retain; otherwise remove or repair just the integration block. If a process was killed and left an `install.lock`, make sure no installer is running before removing that exact lock file and retrying. ## Source and development For stopped local validation, see the bounded [interrupted-run recovery example](evals/resume/INTERRUPTED.md): preserve the failed attempt, validate eligible completed evidence, and rerun unfinished checks in a fresh destination. The full source is included: skill and research references, installer, optional adapter, tests, manifest generator, and release builder. There are no hidden components or npm dependencies. ```sh node scripts/manifest.mjs node scripts/run-checks.mjs python scripts/build_release.py ``` Tests cover installation choices, backups, rollback, package integrity, and the local behavioral evaluation harness, including deliberately incorrect candidates. CI runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux with Node 20, 22, and 24. The included workflows use standard runners, skip private repositories, and add no model API calls or artifact/cache uploads. These checks do not establish reconstruction quality on every target or model. The test runner first checks directory-link fixture setup in the same temporary parent/runtime. A denied or unknown probe leaves required validation incomplete; it does not explain unrelated assertion failures or prove administrator rights are needed. Original test failures and counts remain visible. See [test environment diagnostics](CONTRIBUTING.md#test-environment-diagnostics) for probe-only output, explicit full runs and supported local/CI next steps. The [behavioral evaluation kit](evals/README.md) supplies portable tasks, raw evidence, independent executable oracles, and a human review rubric. It covers narrow functions, file formats, stateful workflows, original quirks versus approved improvements, ambiguous retries, inaccessible backends, contradictory evidence, hostile embedded instructions, cryptographic boundaries, and cost-sensitive tool choices. Paired selection tasks check that an implementation follows the requested compatibility or improvement goal; human review still verifies its reasoning and authorization. Running its harness tests is separate from evaluating an actual agent; model runs are not started automatically and require an environment established to incur no additional charge. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).
Explore evaluation tools and worked examples **Reference app trial (v1.3.0):** [Pocket Tasks and its repeatable procedure](evals/reference/README.md) add a small local app with real saving, restart behavior, and a selection quirk to investigate. Export a separate evidence packet, document observations and requirements, then compare a reviewed reconstruction through a language-independent JSON process interface. The supplied tools use the existing Node runtime without packages, network calls, or model invocations. Self-tests validate the app/checker; actual host and REA trials remain separately recorded, with human review still required. **Evidence verification (v1.3.1):** the packet tool adds a read-only `--verify` command to detect missing or changed reference evidence before and after a trial. It checks against the original trusted package, so rewriting the packet's hashes cannot hide a change. See the [reference procedure](evals/reference/README.md#1-freeze-the-trial-and-prepare-evidence) for its scope and limits. **Worked investigation:** [follow Pocket Tasks from evidence to requirements](evals/reference/WALKTHROUGH.md). The example includes actual REA analysis, seven recorded runtime scenarios, a replay test, and a decision about preserving or improving an awkward behavior. Source/test exposure and incomplete analysis are disclosed. It stops before candidate implementation and is not a model benchmark or a compatibility certification. **Worked reconstruction (v1.3.3):** [continue from those requirements to an implementation and validation](evals/reference/reconstruction/README.md). A standalone local candidate passes the 16-session checker and replays the ten captured observation sessions. The example links requirements to code and tests, records an environment-limited first attempt, and supplies a repeatable validator with evidence-integrity checks. It uses existing Node.js without packages or network/model calls. Prior source and reviewer exposure remain explicit; this teaching example is not an independent evaluation or certification. **Worked browser improvement (v1.3.14):** [preserve parity while improving save feedback and conflict recovery](evals/browser-improvement/README.md). Separate reference, parity and improved fixtures demonstrate failed-save feedback, retained drafts, explicit recovery and overlapping tab writes. The portable example includes acceptance requirements, replay routines and captured results, with cooperative-lock, controlled-injection and same-agent limits. **Checkpoint/resume evaluation (v1.3.4):** [resume unchanged work or reassess a changed target](evals/resume/README.md). Two supplied-evidence cases exercise scoped reuse, partial implementation, preserved history and stale result handling. A local JSON-only checker performs 15 data comparisons per case; actual reasoning, actions and preservation still need human review. The skill includes a portable checkpoint guide, with no memory service, SDK, new dependency or automatic worker. The worked records are disclosed maintainer-authored examples, not cross-host/model certification. **Measured environment example:** [revalidate behavior after a relevant setting changes](evals/resume/environment/README.md). Identical fixture bytes run under two controlled cap settings with a minimal local Node probe. Reports retain unaffected formatter evidence and recheck score/integration behavior. Cross-version drift and cross-host compatibility remain unverified.
## Support the project If this project is useful to you, you can [support my work on Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/shadowswaps). Contributions are optional; the project remains freely available under its open-source licenses.

Bug reports, reproducible examples and focused pull requests are also welcome. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) before contributing. ## License All original code, skill instructions, tests, build scripts, and documentation in this repository are released under the [MIT license](LICENSE). You may use, modify, and redistribute them, including commercially, subject to that license. The evaluation kit includes a small, attributed [Wycheproof test-data subset](evals/fixtures/wycheproof-empty.json) under its bundled [Apache-2.0 license](evals/fixtures/wycheproof-LICENSE.txt); it remains fully open-source. Upstream REA and linked research remain separate projects; no REA code or cryptographic implementation is bundled. No particular AI provider or proprietary model is required by this project.

name: Installer tests
on:
  push:
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    # Standard public-repository runners only; avoid billable private-fork runs.
    if: github.event.repository.visibility == 'public'
    timeout-minutes: 10
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
        node: [20, 22, 24]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@d23441a48e516b6c34aea4fa41551a30e30af803 # v6
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@249970729cb0ef3589644e2896645e5dc5ba9c38 # v6
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      - name: Verify release manifest is current
        run: |
          node scripts/manifest.mjs
          git diff --exit-code -- manifest.json
      - run: node scripts/run-checks.mjs
      - name: Verify and test the release archive
        run: |
          python scripts/build_release.py
          python scripts/verify_release.py
