Expect incremental code changes and validation against observed requirements, with gaps and differences reported: ```text Use REA and the companion to investigate the desktop notes app I have open and build a local web app with similar note creation, editing, search, and save behavior in this workspace. Start with one working workflow, then add the remaining features in testable increments. Validate against the evidence and report differences and anything you could not verify. ``` **Investigate one function or feature.** Expect a focused contract covering inputs, outputs, side effects, errors, and evidence gaps: ```text Use REA and the companion to investigate the CSV import feature in the app I have open. Trace how it handles headers, quoted fields, duplicate rows, and malformed input. Document inputs, outputs, side effects, error behavior, and representative acceptance cases, citing the evidence. Keep this to an investigation; do not implement changes. ``` The agent must report missing tools or evidence instead of claiming live analysis or complete equivalence. A build request does not authorize deployment, releases, installation changes, paid tools, or additional charges. Those actions require their own authority; the no-additional-charges constraint below still applies. ### Continue or optimize a scoped implementation > Continue implementing the app from this project's REA reconstruction specification. > Reimplement the decodeFrame function in this library and make it faster for large inputs. Recover its contract, then compare correctness and performance. ### Resume earlier work > Pick up from this checkpoint. Keep the same scope, retain the passing evidence that still applies, and work on the next unfinished part. Select the checkpoint or its path and identify any changed target or goal. The agent should read that record and the sources needed for the next step, check evidence applicability, and preserve historical results. Resuming a specification does not authorize building it. See [portable checkpoint guidance](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/references/checkpoints.md) and the [worked resume example](evals/resume/WALKTHROUGH.md). For a small question, expect a compact evidence-linked answer or contract with limits and a useful next action. A feature build adds implementation and acceptance results; it need not produce a whole-app blueprint. If a consequential target or outcome is unclear, expect one focused clarification. Host activation and instruction following vary: explicit invocation can help select the skill, but examples and installation do not guarantee every host/model will interpret every phrasing correctly. To see the workflow before trying a target, follow the [worked investigation](evals/reference/WALKTHROUGH.md), [reconstruction](evals/reference/reconstruction/README.md), or [resume](evals/resume/WALKTHROUGH.md) for your goal. These disclose answers and prior source exposure; they are teaching material, not prerequisites or evidence of a fresh agent trial. The [first-use review](evals/first-use.md) separates manual intent scenarios from executable checks. ## What it does - Identifies the requested subject, evidence carrier, and objective from natural language. No form or bracketed prompt variables are required. - Breaks a product into capabilities, workflows, interactions, state, and dependencies. - Defines requirements, contracts, expected behavior, and acceptance criteria linked to evidence. - Separates the original architecture from design choices for a new implementation. - Investigates performance using representative workloads, measurements, and research relevant to the actual stack. - Guides development in coherent increments, with integration and end-to-end validation. - Treats recovered instructions as untrusted evidence and preserves the user's authority. - Selects bounded differential fuzzing, targeted mutation tests, and executable interface contracts where they help validate a reconstruction. - Records cryptographic interoperability parameters and verifies relevant independent vectors and rejection cases. - Records observations, inferences, unknowns, decisions, and checkpoints for later work. ## How it works with REA REA supplies the reverse-engineering tools and evidence workflow. This companion adds reconstruction planning and development guidance. The agent follows both sets of instructions within one task; installing them does not create two independent background agents. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[User goal and target] --> B[Scope and questions] B --> C[REA evidence] C --> D[Requirements and design] D --> E[Implementation when requested] E --> F[Validation and measurements] D -->|Evidence gap| C F -->|Evidence gap| C ``` For the method and its sources, see the [skill instructions](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/SKILL.md) and [research basis](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/references/research-basis.md). ## Install Download and extract the ZIP from [Releases](https://github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion/releases), or clone this repository. Run commands from the extracted folder or repository root. On Windows, macOS, and Linux, the installer commands are the same. For automatic co-use, first install [REA for your client](https://github.com/morluto/rea#readme). Then choose a command: ```sh # Claude Code, with the optional integration node install.mjs --client claude-code --integration on # Codex, with the optional integration node install.mjs --client codex --integration on # Companion only; no changes to REA node install.mjs --client claude-code --integration off ``` Use `--dry-run` on any installation command to inspect the paths and changes without writing files. The `companionChanges` lists identify added, modified, and removed files relative to the companion directory, including local files that a replacement would move into the backup. Use the same command with `--check` afterward to verify the selected installation mode. A missing REA skill or ambiguous choice stops integrated installation before the companion is installed. Differently cased paths to the same REA file are treated as one candidate; genuinely separate installations still require an explicit selection. `claude_code`, as used by REA, is accepted as an alias for `claude-code` by the installer and updater. Plans, receipts and newly saved update settings use `claude-code`.
Client paths, custom profiles and advanced installation Default user locations: - Claude Code: `~/.claude/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/`, or `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/` when a custom configuration directory is set in the installer's environment. See [Claude Code's environment-variable documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars). REA lookup stays within that selected profile unless `--rea-skill` explicitly selects another location. - Codex: `~/.agents/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/`, or `$CODEX_HOME/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/` when `CODEX_HOME` is set. The installer also checks the older `~/.codex/skills/` location when locating REA. - Generic clients: specify their documented skills directory with `--skills-dir`. Override paths for an existing installation, a project-scoped skill, or another agent: ```sh node install.mjs --client generic --integration on --skills-dir "/path/to/skills" --rea-skill "/path/to/reverse-engineer-anything/SKILL.md" ``` `--skills-dir` accepts the parent skills directory; the installer creates `rea-reconstruction-companion` beneath it. It takes precedence over client defaults and environment variables. The REA path must identify the skill actually loaded by that client. An override disables broad automatic lookup. Paths with spaces should be quoted. If the installer runs outside the agent's environment, supply that agent's actual directory explicitly. Keep the downloaded package or checkout separate from the installation destination. The installer rejects overlapping source/destination directories and a REA file inside the companion destination, including existing paths that differ only by casing on a filesystem that treats them as the same location. The optional `agents/openai.yaml` adapter is installed only for Codex. The portable core and Claude Code installation do not depend on it. Refresh the host's skills or start a fresh session if the new skill is not visible.
## Optional REA integration Choose one during installation: | Choice | What the installer does | When it helps | | --- | --- | --- | | `--integration on` | Adds a marked instruction block to your selected REA `SKILL.md`. | When you want relevant REA reconstruction requests to load the companion without naming it separately. | | `--integration off` | Installs only the companion and leaves REA untouched. | When you prefer explicitly invoking the companion or managing your own routing rules. | The integration asks the agent to use the companion for understanding a target **for reconstruction**, planning a similar implementation, or rebuilding selected functionality. Its benefits are shared evidence, a consistent requirements-to-test trail, and focused returns to REA when design or testing exposes an unanswered question. Ordinary explanations, comparisons, and diagnostics stay narrow. This is an instruction-based integration. It does not override client policies, grant tool permissions, connect MCP servers, guarantee model compliance, or force parallel execution. Without the rule, invoking the companion still tells the agent to use REA. The rule supplies the reverse direction: relevant REA work also loads the companion. **REA skill refreshes can remove this rule.** In REA 6.5.0 (skill version 42), `rea doctor` requires byte-for-byte canonical skill files, so adding our block can produce `skill:identity` / `config_drift` with “Installed REA skill identity is stale” even when version and tool count match. This is a known cause, not a reason to ignore all stale or doctor diagnostics: other managed files or settings may also differ. The pinned [identity check](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/3b79af28e80785afce9f5998d8f03289402a1847/src/application/Doctor.ts) and [skill installer](https://github.com/morluto/rea/blob/3b79af28e80785afce9f5998d8f03289402a1847/src/application/SetupSkill.ts) show why `rea setup` restores canonical files and preserves edited originals in backups, removing the active companion block. An REA update that refreshes the skill can do the same; other upstream versions may differ. After `rea setup`, `rea update`, or another REA skill refresh, recheck the selected integration and, if needed, restore only its block using the matching verified companion package; see [verification and scoped recovery](INSTALL.md#verify-and-report). Do not restore an entire old REA backup over newer instructions. If routing disappeared, explicitly invoke the companion or run the manual check. The optional on-use warning cannot run if the companion/helper is never invoked. `off` means **do not manage REA**, not “remove a rule already installed.” To disable an earlier integration, remove only the block between `` and `` in the selected REA `SKILL.md`, including the markers. Keep the rest of REA intact. ## Requirements and compatibility The core skill is plain Markdown in the [Agent Skills format](https://agentskills.io/specification). It has no model SDK, paid API requirement, Python dependency, telemetry, or background service. ### No additional charges The skill forbids initiating actions that could add charges: purchases, subscriptions/trials, metered APIs or model calls, billable cloud/CI/storage/deployment, and indirect paid work. Existing local tools and supplied evidence come first. If an action's no-charge status cannot be established for the actual environment, the agent must skip it and explain a local alternative or limitation. An available tool or a free tier is not sufficient evidence. It does not automatically launch agents, evaluations, or scheduled jobs. This rule is an instruction, not a billing enforcement mechanism. An AI host may itself bill tokens or usage credits, and local execution consumes resources such as electricity. The skill cannot guarantee zero total cost or control another product's billing or model compliance. It must not enable extra paid usage or alter billing settings; use host/account spending controls for an absolute spending limit. No paid exception is part of this skill's workflow. | Component | Requirement | | --- | --- | | Skill workflow | A capable agent that can read the skill and its references; REA tools or supplied REA evidence for actual investigation. | | Included installer | Node.js 20 or newer. Uses only Node's standard library; no `npm install`, PyYAML, or network access. | | Optional update helper (v1.2.0+) | Existing Node.js 20+. Uses the standard library and opt-in public GitHub requests; no packages, tokens, model calls or scheduler. | | REA | Installed and configured separately for your client. REA and target-specific engines have their own requirements. | | Release building | Python 3.10+ standard library, for maintainers only. Not needed to install or use the skill. | Codex and Claude Code both support filesystem skills. Their discovery locations and invocation syntax differ; the installer handles those differences. Other agents can use the same core files through an explicit skills directory. Compatibility depends on the host's file/tool access, not just the model name. See the official [Codex skill documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills) and [Claude Code skill documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills). Hosted uploads and chat-only clients are different: an uploaded skill ZIP cannot generally edit a separate local REA installation. Supply both skills and evidence through that host's supported mechanisms, or use a local agent for installation and live analysis. No live-model compatibility certification is implied by the installer tests. ## Optional weekly update checks (since v1.2.0) Starting with **v1.2.0**, the updater is bundled inside the skill, including installations for Codex, Claude Code and generic clients. Enable it once after installation if you want release notifications. The host calls a small local helper when the skill is used; it contacts GitHub only when seven days have elapsed. An idle skill runs nothing. Earlier versions do not gain this automatically: manually install a published v1.2.0-or-later package first. With checks enabled and recorded integration on, the current helper also inspects the recorded REA rule locally before cooldown or network decisions. Missing, changed/malformed, or unreadable/unsafe rules return `integration-needs-attention` without repair, state changes or networking. Disabled checks and integration off do not inspect REA. This warning is available only in versions containing this change and only when the companion/helper is invoked; it is not a background monitor or a full `rea doctor` check. When a newer stable release is found, the agent offers **Update now / Remind me next week / Skip this version / Disable checks**. No answer means no update. Approval is tied to the offered release and asset; changed assets require a new offer. Local customizations stop automatic replacement. Successful updates retain backups, verify the result and preserve your selected client and REA integration setting. Checks are **off by default**, independent of integration, and require existing Node.js 20+. There is no npm dependency, model/API key, paid service, extra model call, background daemon or scheduled AI task. Online operations also require confirmation that the actual network/tool environment cannot add charges. Unknown-cost or unavailable access is skipped; this is not an unconditional zero-resource-cost or billing-enforcement guarantee. Read the [setup, commands, state location and recovery guide](skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/references/updates.md). Host instruction-following and local command access are required; the helper cannot force every AI host to invoke it or authenticate a human response. Installation refresh behavior depends on the host. The project owner's release approval process remains unchanged. ## Updates, backups, and recovery - Repeating the same installation is safe and does not duplicate the integration block. - Differing companion files require `--replace`; the installer backs up the entire prior companion directory before replacing it. - REA edits preserve everything outside the marked integration block. The exact earlier pre-release rule can also be migrated; customized unmarked rules require review. - Backups and a receipt are stored in `.rea-reconstruction-companion-installer/` next to the parent skills directory. The installer prints the exact transaction path. - Failed commits attempt REA and companion recovery independently, so an unreadable or missing REA file does not prevent restoring the prior companion. Backups remain available; a detected concurrent edit is retained and reported rather than overwritten. - Updating REA may replace its skill instructions. Follow [verification and scoped recovery](INSTALL.md#verify-and-report) after a refresh. Nothing monitors or rewrites REA in the background. For manual recovery, use the printed receipt to locate the selected paths. Restore `companion-before` to the companion's former location if appropriate. Restore `rea-before.md` only when REA has no later changes you need to retain; otherwise remove or repair just the integration block. If a process was killed and left an `install.lock`, make sure no installer is running before removing that exact lock file and retrying. ## Source and development For stopped local validation, see the bounded [interrupted-run recovery example](evals/resume/INTERRUPTED.md): preserve the failed attempt, validate eligible completed evidence, and rerun unfinished checks in a fresh destination. The full source is included: skill and research references, installer, optional adapter, tests, manifest generator, and release builder. There are no hidden components or npm dependencies. ```sh node scripts/manifest.mjs node scripts/run-checks.mjs python scripts/build_release.py ``` Tests cover installation choices, backups, rollback, package integrity, and the local behavioral evaluation harness, including deliberately incorrect candidates. CI runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux with Node 20, 22, and 24. The included workflows use standard runners, skip private repositories, and add no model API calls or artifact/cache uploads. These checks do not establish reconstruction quality on every target or model. The test runner first checks directory-link fixture setup in the same temporary parent/runtime. A denied or unknown probe leaves required validation incomplete; it does not explain unrelated assertion failures or prove administrator rights are needed. Original test failures and counts remain visible. See [test environment diagnostics](CONTRIBUTING.md#test-environment-diagnostics) for probe-only output, explicit full runs and supported local/CI next steps. The [behavioral evaluation kit](evals/README.md) supplies portable tasks, raw evidence, independent executable oracles, and a human review rubric. It covers narrow functions, file formats, stateful workflows, original quirks versus approved improvements, ambiguous retries, inaccessible backends, contradictory evidence, hostile embedded instructions, cryptographic boundaries, and cost-sensitive tool choices. Paired selection tasks check that an implementation follows the requested compatibility or improvement goal; human review still verifies its reasoning and authorization. Running its harness tests is separate from evaluating an actual agent; model runs are not started automatically and require an environment established to incur no additional charge. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).
Explore evaluation tools and worked examples **Reference app trial (v1.3.0):** [Pocket Tasks and its repeatable procedure](evals/reference/README.md) add a small local app with real saving, restart behavior, and a selection quirk to investigate. Export a separate evidence packet, document observations and requirements, then compare a reviewed reconstruction through a language-independent JSON process interface. The supplied tools use the existing Node runtime without packages, network calls, or model invocations. Self-tests validate the app/checker; actual host and REA trials remain separately recorded, with human review still required. **Evidence verification (v1.3.1):** the packet tool adds a read-only `--verify` command to detect missing or changed reference evidence before and after a trial. It checks against the original trusted package, so rewriting the packet's hashes cannot hide a change. See the [reference procedure](evals/reference/README.md#1-freeze-the-trial-and-prepare-evidence) for its scope and limits. **Worked investigation:** [follow Pocket Tasks from evidence to requirements](evals/reference/WALKTHROUGH.md). The example includes actual REA analysis, seven recorded runtime scenarios, a replay test, and a decision about preserving or improving an awkward behavior. Source/test exposure and incomplete analysis are disclosed. It stops before candidate implementation and is not a model benchmark or a compatibility certification. **Worked reconstruction (v1.3.3):** [continue from those requirements to an implementation and validation](evals/reference/reconstruction/README.md). A standalone local candidate passes the 16-session checker and replays the ten captured observation sessions. The example links requirements to code and tests, records an environment-limited first attempt, and supplies a repeatable validator with evidence-integrity checks. It uses existing Node.js without packages or network/model calls. Prior source and reviewer exposure remain explicit; this teaching example is not an independent evaluation or certification. **Worked browser improvement (v1.3.14):** [preserve parity while improving save feedback and conflict recovery](evals/browser-improvement/README.md). Separate reference, parity and improved fixtures demonstrate failed-save feedback, retained drafts, explicit recovery and overlapping tab writes. The portable example includes acceptance requirements, replay routines and captured results, with cooperative-lock, controlled-injection and same-agent limits. **Checkpoint/resume evaluation (v1.3.4):** [resume unchanged work or reassess a changed target](evals/resume/README.md). Two supplied-evidence cases exercise scoped reuse, partial implementation, preserved history and stale result handling. A local JSON-only checker performs 15 data comparisons per case; actual reasoning, actions and preservation still need human review. The skill includes a portable checkpoint guide, with no memory service, SDK, new dependency or automatic worker. The worked records are disclosed maintainer-authored examples, not cross-host/model certification. **Measured environment example:** [revalidate behavior after a relevant setting changes](evals/resume/environment/README.md). Identical fixture bytes run under two controlled cap settings with a minimal local Node probe. Reports retain unaffected formatter evidence and recheck score/integration behavior. Cross-version drift and cross-host compatibility remain unverified.
## Support the project If this project is useful to you, you can [support my work on Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/shadowswaps). Contributions are optional; the project remains freely available under its open-source licenses.

Bug reports, reproducible examples and focused pull requests are also welcome. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) before contributing. ## License All original code, skill instructions, tests, build scripts, and documentation in this repository are released under the [MIT license](LICENSE). You may use, modify, and redistribute them, including commercially, subject to that license. The evaluation kit includes a small, attributed [Wycheproof test-data subset](evals/fixtures/wycheproof-empty.json) under its bundled [Apache-2.0 license](evals/fixtures/wycheproof-LICENSE.txt); it remains fully open-source. Upstream REA and linked research remain separate projects; no REA code or cryptographic implementation is bundled. No particular AI provider or proprietary model is required by this project.

# Agentic Engineering Toolkit (AE Toolkit) **AE Toolkit is a process, not a collection of prompts.** Most AI coding sessions start strong and end in drift. The agent builds what it _assumed_, not what you _meant_. Context degrades after a few tasks. The same bug shows up next week because the system never learned. There is no workflow — just vibes and hope. AE Toolkit fixes this by encoding the best agentic engineering patterns from YC, Garry Tan (GStack), Matt Pocock, and the AI Transformation Workshop into a modular skill suite. Every request is classified by **work class** (trivial / normal / critical) before any skill runs, so a typo fix doesn't endure full PRD ceremony and an auth rewrite doesn't slip through with mocked tests alone: **Triage → Plan → Design → Validate → Prime → Implement → QA → Review → Ship → Evolve** `/aet-prime` classifies the request and routes it to the appropriate pipeline. Trivial tasks ship in minutes. Normal tasks get lightweight plans. Critical tasks (auth, data, infrastructure, upgrades) run the full sequence including `/aet-verify` — observed evidence that the system actually works before merge. `/aet-plan` writes a PRD. `/aet-design-system-creation` produces DESIGN.md — your design source of truth. `/aet-validate-scope` checks the plan and design against your existing domain model and documented decisions before a single line of code is written. `/aet-implement` reads the plan — with `/aet-tdd` optionally guiding test-first development. `/aet-review` catches what `/aet-implement` missed. `/aet-qa` verifies the fix. `/aet-ship` gates the merge. `/aet-evolve` updates the rules so the bug never repeats. Nothing falls through the cracks because every step knows what came before it. ## What you get - **Proportionate ceremony** — `aet-prime` classifies every request into trivial, normal, or critical work. A typo ships in minutes; auth changes run the full pipeline - **Shared understanding before code** — `aet-plan` asks targeted questions until the agent actually gets it, before it writes a PRD - **Validate against reality before you build** — `aet-validate-scope` catches terminology conflicts, code contradictions, and architectural misalignment while they're still cheap to fix - **Observed evidence for critical work** — `aet-verify` exercises the running system and captures proof (HTTP response, screenshot, CLI output) before merge - **Test-first development** — `aet-tdd` guides red-green-refactor with vertical tracer bullets and integration-style tests that survive refactors - **Fresh-session implementation** — plans and code never share a context window; bias can't leak - **Night-shift productivity** — `aet run` grinds through your curated task queue while you sleep, clearing context between each ticket so quality doesn't degrade. Tasks only close with evidence, and runs shut down cleanly on timeout - **A local dashboard for your work** — the telemetry panel lets you browse plans, watch pipeline progress, and review run history without digging through files - **One-command full flows** — `aet-pipeline-plan` runs the entire planning sequence; `aet run` runs the full implementation sequence with session-isolated stages - **Dependency upgrades as first-class work** — `aet-plan`'s upgrade planning analyzes breaking changes, maps risk, and marks the plan critical so smoke runs before and after you bump a framework version - **Compounding quality** — every bug updates a rule, template, or guardrail in `.agents/`. The system gets smarter across sessions, not just within them. - **Agent-agnostic** — works with Claude Code, Kimi, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, or paste-into-chat. Your workflow is portable. ### Who it's for - **Solo developers** who want agentic workflows without building them from scratch - **Engineering leads** who want consistent planning, review, and shipping standards across a team - **AI-native startups** who treat the AI layer (rules, commands, skills) as first-class infrastructure --- ## How the pieces fit together AE Toolkit has three layers. **Skills decide, the `aet` CLI does, and state remembers.** Your agent reads the skills to make judgment calls; the skills direct the agent to run `aet` CLI commands for anything mechanical; the CLI is the single writer for the queue, telemetry, and git state. ```mermaid flowchart TB A["1 · Skills — the workflow brain
aet-plan · aet-prime · aet-implement · aet-review
aet-qa · aet-ship · aet-evolve · …
Your agent reads these to decide and judge"] B["2 · aet CLI — the operational hands
aet run · aet next · aet sprint add · aet state
aet status · aet ship · aet retro · aet mine-learnings
Deterministic commands that do the mechanical work"] C["3 · State — the memory
Task queue (local JSON · git-refs · GitHub Issues)
Telemetry archive · Git worktrees and branches
Where work and evidence live"] A -->|"skill directs the agent to run CLI commands"| B B -->|"reads and writes"| C C -->|"state and results flow back"| A ``` | Layer | Responsible for | You invoke it by | | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | **Skills** (`aet-*`) | Judgment and workflow — triage, planning, review, QA, quality gates | Your agent: `/aet-plan` or natural language | | **`aet` CLI** | Deterministic operations — queue management, orchestration, state transitions, telemetry mining | Your terminal: `aet run`, `aet state`, `aet ship` | | **State** | Persistence — the task queue, telemetry archive, git worktrees | Indirectly, through the CLI | This is why `aet plan` doesn't exist: planning is judgment — a skill your agent runs — not an operation. The CLI only owns mechanical, repeatable work, and because it's the single writer for queue and state transitions, unattended runs can't corrupt state. --- ## Quick Start AE Toolkit has two parts: the **Python CLI package** (`aet`) and the **skill instructions** your agent reads. You need both for the pipeline to work. ### One-line install (macOS/Linux) The installer bootstraps `uv`, clones the repo, installs the `aet` CLI into a dedicated venv, links skills into detected agent directories, and symlinks `aet` onto `PATH`: ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thebrightnest/ae-toolkit/main/scripts/install.sh | bash ``` Target a specific agent, preview changes, or pin a release: ```bash # Target one agent directory explicitly curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thebrightnest/ae-toolkit/main/scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --agent claude-code # Preview every planned action without making changes curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thebrightnest/ae-toolkit/main/scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --dry-run # Install a specific tag curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thebrightnest/ae-toolkit/main/scripts/install.sh | bash -s -- --tag v1.21.0 ``` #### Installer options | Flag | Description | Example | | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | | `--tag ` | Install a tagged release (default: latest semver tag, falling back to `main`) | `--tag v1.21.0` | | `--agent ` | Target one agent directory: `claude-code`, `kimi`, `cursor`, or `generic` | `--agent claude-code` | | `--bin-dir ` | Target `PATH` directory for the `aet` symlink (default: `~/.local/bin`) | `--bin-dir ~/.bin` | | `--skills-dir ` | Override the skills directory (default: auto-detect) | `--skills-dir ~/.claude/skills` | | `--repo ` | Clone from a different source (default: GitHub main repo) | `--repo /path/to/local/clone` | | `--dry-run` | Print planned actions without making changes | `--dry-run` | #### Troubleshooting **`aet` command not found after install.** The installer symlinks `aet` into `~/.local/bin` (or the directory you passed to `--bin-dir`). If that directory is not on your `PATH`, add it to your shell profile: ```bash # bash/zsh echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc # or ~/.zshrc ``` Then reload your profile (`source ~/.bashrc` or `source ~/.zshrc`) or open a new shell. **`aet` runs a different copy than the one you installed.** If another `aet` is earlier on your `PATH`, the installer prints a warning naming the shadowing path and still exits 0. Run `aet setup verify` at any time to see which copy `aet` resolves to and whether it matches the expected install: ```bash aet setup verify ``` `verify` also reports whether the installed version is the newest release. It never edits `PATH`, shell profiles, or the link. **A skill you no longer have still shows up in your agent.** When a release retires a skill, its symlink is left pointing at nothing. `aet setup skills` (and `aet update`, which runs it) removes links to toolkit skills that no longer exist. Skills installed with `npx skills add` have to be deleted by hand. ### Manual install If you prefer not to run the curl installer, install the Python package and skills separately: #### 1. Install the Python package ```bash # Latest release from source pip install git+https://github.com/thebrightnest/ae-toolkit.git@v1.21.0 ``` #### 2. Install the skills `aet setup skills` links every toolkit skill and removes links to skills that no longer exist: ```bash # Auto-detect installed agents and link skills to all of them aet setup skills # Target a specific agent directory aet setup skills --agent claude-code # Use a custom skills directory aet setup skills --skills-dir ~/.claude/skills ``` Or install skills via `npx`: ```bash npx skills add https://github.com/thebrightnest/ae-toolkit --all ``` #### 3. Put `aet` on `PATH` ```bash aet setup link ``` The command symlinks `aet` into `~/.local/bin` (override with `AET_BIN_DIR`). If `~/.local/bin` is not on your `PATH`, add it to your shell profile. The link is no longer self-healing; re-run the installer or `aet setup link` if it breaks. # Agentic Engineering Toolkit (AE Toolkit) **AE Toolkit is a process, not a collection of prompts.** Most AI coding sessions start strong and end in drift. The agent builds what it _assumed_, not what you _meant_. Context degrades after a few tasks. The same bug shows up next week because the system never learned. There is no workflow — just vibes and hope. AE Toolkit fixes this by encoding the best agentic engineering patterns from YC, Garry Tan (GStack), Matt Pocock, and the AI Transformation Workshop into a modular skill suite. Every request is classified by **work class** (trivial / normal / critical) before any skill runs, so a typo fix doesn't endure full PRD ceremony and an auth rewrite doesn't slip through with mocked tests alone: **Triage → Plan → Design → Validate → Prime → Implement → QA → Review → Ship → Evolve** `/aet-prime` classifies the request and routes it to the appropriate pipeline. Trivial tasks ship in minutes. Normal tasks get lightweight plans. Critical tasks (auth, data, infrastructure, upgrades) run the full sequence including `/aet-verify` — observed evidence that the system actually works before merge. `/aet-plan` writes a PRD. `/aet-design-system-creation` produces DESIGN.md — your design source of truth. `/aet-validate-scope` checks the plan and design against your existing domain model and documented decisions before a single line of code is written. `/aet-implement` reads the plan — with `/aet-tdd` optionally guiding test-first development. `/aet-review` catches what `/aet-implement` missed. `/aet-qa` verifies the fix. `/aet-ship` gates the merge. `/aet-evolve` updates the rules so the bug never repeats. Nothing falls through the cracks because every step knows what came before it. ## What you get - **Proportionate ceremony** — `aet-prime` classifies every request into trivial, normal, or critical work. A typo ships in minutes; auth changes run the full pipeline - **Shared understanding before code** — `aet-plan` asks targeted questions until the agent actually gets it, before it writes a PRD - **Validate against reality before you build** — `aet-validate-scope` catches terminology conflicts, code contradictions, and architectural misalignment while they're still cheap to fix - **Observed evidence for critical work** — `aet-verify` exercises the running system and captures proof (HTTP response, screenshot, CLI output) before merge - **Test-first development** — `aet-tdd` guides red-green-refactor with vertical tracer bullets and integration-style tests that survive refactors - **Fresh-session implementation** — plans and code never share a context window; bias can't leak - **Night-shift productivity** — `aet run` grinds through your curated task queue while you sleep, clearing context between each ticket so quality doesn't degrade. Tasks only close with evidence, and runs shut down cleanly on timeout - **A local dashboard for your work** — the telemetry panel lets you browse plans, watch pipeline progress, and review run history without digging through files - **One-command full flows** — `aet-pipeline-plan` runs the entire planning sequence; `aet run` runs the full implementation sequence with session-isolated stages - **Dependency upgrades as first-class work** — `aet-plan`'s upgrade planning analyzes breaking changes, maps risk, and marks the plan critical so smoke runs before and after you bump a framework version - **Compounding quality** — every bug updates a rule, template, or guardrail in `.agents/`. The system gets smarter across sessions, not just within them. - **Agent-agnostic** — works with Claude Code, Kimi, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, or paste-into-chat. Your workflow is portable. ### Who it's for - **Solo developers** who want agentic workflows without building them from scratch - **Engineering leads** who want consistent planning, review, and shipping standards across a team - **AI-native startups** who treat the AI layer (rules, commands, skills) as first-class infrastructure --- ## How the pieces fit together AE Toolkit has three layers. **Skills decide, the `aet` CLI does, and state remembers.** Your agent reads the skills to make judgment calls; the skills direct the agent to run `aet` CLI commands for anything mechanical; the CLI is the single writer for the queue, telemetry, and git state. ```mermaid flowchart TB A["1 · Skills — the workflow brain
aet-plan · aet-prime · aet-implement · aet-review
aet-qa · aet-ship · aet-evolve · …
Your agent reads these to decide and judge"] B["2 · aet CLI — the operational hands
aet run · aet next · aet sprint add · aet state
aet status · aet ship · aet retro · aet mine-learnings
Deterministic commands that do the mechanical work"] C["3 · State — the memory
Task queue (local JSON · git-refs · GitHub Issues)
Telemetry archive · Git worktrees and branches
Where work and evidence live"] A -->|"skill directs the agent to run CLI commands"| B B -->|"reads and writes"| C C -->|"state and results flow back"| A ``` | Layer | Responsible for | You invoke it by | | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | | **Skills** (`aet-*`) | Judgment and workflow — triage, planning, review, QA, quality gates | Your agent: `/aet-plan` or natural language | | **`aet` CLI** | Deterministic operations — queue management, orchestration, state transitions, telemetry mining | Your terminal: `aet run`, `aet state`, `aet ship` | | **State** | Persistence — the task queue, telemetry archive, git worktrees | Indirectly, through the CLI | This is why `aet plan` doesn't exist: planning is judgment — a skill your agent runs — not an operation. repository.readme:
# graff

A code map for Claude Code, built without models. Of three tools for Claude
Code, ekko keeps the why, ctx keeps the cost down, and graff is to say where:
where a symbol is defined, what calls it and what it calls, what a file
holds and on which lines, a search ranked by BM25, and a map of what
matters most ranked by personalized PageRank, every answer within a token
budget, from an index that re-parses
what changed on each query. Its languages are the ones used here: Rust, Nix,
Bash, Python, C and Markdown.

## Status

graff reads Rust, Nix, Bash, Python, C and Markdown: definitions, calls,
references and use items, each with its lines (`src/extract/`), kept in an
index in `~/.cache/graff` that each query will bring up to date by itself,
reading again only what changed (`src/store.rs`). It ties each call and
reference to the definition it reaches, by Rust's rules for names rather
than by types, a file being the module of each `mod` item that loads it as
rustc finds it, through a `path` attribute too, and says what stays
ambiguous (`src/resolve.rs`). A method called on `self` reaches its type's;
one called on anything else, the crate's only method of that name, unless a
type of std has one too or it is the method the call is in, and else, as
possible, those of the crate's and of the libraries of the worktree's other
packages it names in a path or a use item. In Nix, by
its syntax, each binding is a definition named by its path, a NixOS option
declared with mkOption one too, and a file one, which a path imports: a name
is tied to the `let` or `rec` binding it is bound to, a path to its file (a
folder a `builtins.readDir` function lists to what it lists), `inputs.x` to
the flake's input, and a binding to the option of the worktree it sets
(`src/resolve/nix.rs`), but one in what a function of nixpkgs makes a
package, a file or a string of, `pkgs.writeText`'s or `builtins.toJSON`'s,
which sets none; a submodule's option is under the option whose type it
is, wherever the declarations that name the submodule put it. A helper of
the worktree a module calls,
`myLib.mkSys { name = "x"; .. }`, is followed into and evaluated as far as a
module's shape goes, so what it declares and sets stands in the calling
file, as the module system files it (`src/resolve/nix/instance.rs`); the
index keeps what that makes, and where the options it and the files declare
are, until a Nix file or graff's build changes. In
Bash, a file with no extension is told by its shebang or, with none, by the
Emacs mode or the shellcheck directive at its top; a script's functions, the
variables it assigns, one at the first assignment of each name (an
environment variable when the script exports it), and the sections its
comment banners open (`# --- title ---`) are definitions, and so is the
script, which a `.` sources and a command runs. A call is tied to a function
of its own file, else of the files it runs with by `.` (what it sources and,
for a library, the scripts that source it), else to the only function of
that name in the worktree; a variable to its file's, those files', or one
another script exports to the commands it runs. Bash's scope is dynamic: a
variable a function uses with no `local` of its own is tied to the local of
the nearest functions up its callers that declare it, `F.x`, a definition
where another function may reach it: one of its file that uses the name,
or one of another file, where its file sources one or F runs a command its
file does not define. A path is evaluated where it
names the script's own folder (`dirname "$0"`, `${BASH_SOURCE%/*}`, `$(cd ..
&& pwd)`) or named by a `# shellcheck source=` directive
(`src/extract/bash.rs`, `src/resolve/bash.rs`). In Python, a file with no
extension is told by a shebang that runs python, python3 or python3.N; a
module's functions, classes and methods, the names it and its classes
assign, an attribute a method sets through `self` (its class's), and the
module itself are definitions (`src/extract/python.rs`). A name is tied by

it to or a star import brings. A relative import is found through its
package, and an absolute one in the folders a `sys.path.insert` adds,
evaluated from `__file__`, then the importing file's folder and those above
it, the worktree's `src/`, and those a `sys.path.append` adds, a package's
module looking in the top and `src/` before its own folder; a module's
submodule is also what its top puts in `sys.modules` under its name,
`collections.abc` in Python 3.14. A path is
followed through modules and classes, and through a variable a module or a
class assigns a name or a path and nothing else, `Pen = Turtle`, as through
what that names, a class's base and a type included, and through a
function's local given a name or a path alone, `h = self.helper`; `self.f()`
and `super().f()` reach the method of the class or of a base, in Python's
method resolution order, where
a member a class declares with a type, `pos: int` or a def, comes before one
a class only assigns, as pyright reads it, and `self.f` reaches too each
subclass's own `f`, what Python runs where the instance is of it (rule
`override`, which pyright does not tie); a method called on what a class of
the worktree made reaches that class's, and one called on anything else, the
worktree's only method of that name, unless a type of Python's library has
one too. Of the definitions a scope gives one
name and the imports that bind it there, a name reaches the first in no
branch of an `if` false on the host, as pyright reads `sys.platform` and
`os.name`, as a name the module assigns such a test once reads, or as the
host's CPython lacks a module only some platforms build (`msvcrt`, `pwd`),
or false where the name is used, an `else`'s for code in the
`if`'s block (`src/resolve/python.rs`). In C, a
file's functions, variables, structs, unions and enums (by the tag, else by
the typedef that names one), enumerators, typedefs and macros, those a
function defines for itself among them, the prototypes of what it does not
define, and the file are definitions, `static` keeping one to its file; what
only a C++ compiler reads and GCC's attributes are blanked before the parse,
each line keeping its number (`src/extract/c.rs`). `#include "x.h"` is tied
to the x.h in the including file's folder, else to the one file of the
worktree whose path ends so, with no build file read; a name to its file's
definition, else to one in what the file includes or, for a header, in what
includes it, else to the only one not `static` the linker would find, and a
prototype to the definition it declares; a definition in a branch of an
`#if` the build leaves out is none, by what the host's compiler predefines
and what the file and those it includes define, a header's include guard
among them, and the values a condition compares and computes; what a
build's flags decide stays ambiguous
(`src/resolve/c.rs`). In

definitions, a heading's section running to the next heading of its level
or a higher one, named by its text and by the anchor GitHub gives it
(`src/extract/markdown.rs`). A link to a place of the worktree, a path
written in a code span or in the prose (`src/store.rs:120`), and a name a
code span writes as code names one (`Storage::load`, `k3_mmw()`,
`CTX_MIN`, not a bare `kind`) are tied to the file, the section, the
definition holding the line, or the one definition out of test code
whose full name ends as written; a Rust file stands for the `mod` items
that load it (`src/resolve/markdown.rs`). It answers seven
questions (`src/query.rs`):

    graff def Storage::load        # its lines, doc, signature, a type's impl blocks
    graff callers Storage::load    # what reaches it, by the definition each use is in
    graff callees Storage::load    # what it reaches
    graff outline src/store.rs     # what a file defines, nested, with its lines
    graff impact Storage::load     # its callers, theirs, and so on, 3 levels deep
    graff search open store        # the definitions those words find, best first
    graff map src/store.rs         # what matters most around it, by file, 1,024 tokens

with its file (`src/store.rs:Storage::load`) or by a line
(`src/store.rs:120`); a Nix file, a script, a Python module, a C file or a
Markdown one by its path (`src/lib/ledger.sh`, `k3.h`), whose callers are
what imports, sources, includes or links to it; a Rust file by its path
too, whose callers are the links and mentions of its module; and a
Markdown section by its heading, its anchor, or its file and anchor
(`Stable ids`, `stable-ids`, `readme.md#stable-ids`), by the first two only
where no code definition has the name. `def` gives a C
function's definition before its prototypes, which a budget cuts first.
`search` ranks definitions by BM25 over the words of their names, the rest
of their qualified names, their paths and their docs, an identifier split
at underscores and where its case says a word starts and kept whole too, a
word in a name counting five times, as Zoekt counts one, and test code
keeping half its score (`src/search.rs`); it gives 20 unless `--limit` says
how many. It finds nothing, rather than what shares a common word with the
question, when its best match holds too little of it: two of the
question's words, or all when it has fewer, or words that weigh by idf as
much as one only a definition alone holds, stop words aside; the answer
then names the words the best holds and those none does. `map` is Aider's repository map: the worktree's definitions
ranked by PageRank over the graph of the uses that tie them, from the
definition a use is in to the one it reaches, a use that may reach one of
several definitions weighing a tenth and one that may reach a type of std
or of Python's library none (`src/rank.rs`); each by its signature under its
file's path, the files best first, cut to 1,024 tokens unless `--budget`
says otherwise. Named files and symbols are its focus, which it leaves out:
the walk jumps to them rather than anywhere, so the map gives what they
lean on. Resolving every use of the worktree takes most of a first map,
so the graph is kept in the index, for the worktree's files and the build,
and read back by the next map until a file changes. On ekko at f9564f4
(4,799 definitions) a map took 0.09 to 0.11 s with the graph kept and
0.38 to 0.40 s making it, on kmux at 5377be7 (15,984) 0.27 s and 1.56 to
1.58 s, on Python 3.14's library (33,403) 0.41 to 0.42 s and 1.10 to
1.11 s, and on nixpkgs's nixos/modules at 71dd4e4 (116,641) 1.29 to
1.32 s and 2.43 to 2.49 s, against 0.36 to 0.38, 1.49 to 1.52, 1.04 to
1.05 and 2.37 to 2.45 s before the graph was kept, and 0.05, 0.11, 0.15
and 0.41 to 0.42 s for `outline` (five runs each, interleaved,
2026-10-12, on AC with TLP's balanced profile, the CPU's boost off, the
load at 5 to 16 from other sessions). On nixos/modules most of what is
left is writing a line for each of its definitions before the budget cuts
them. `search` does not use the graph: on the
probe of `evals/search/`, ordering its results by a walk from them, or
adding their rank to their score, did no better than BM25 alone.
An answer is cut to `--budget` tokens, 2,000 unless told, counted as 4
bytes each, least important lines first, and its last line says what it
left out and the budget that would hold it all; `--json` gives the same
answer as one object. Uses graff cannot tie to one definition, mostly
method calls on what it cannot tell the type of, are listed apart as
possible. On ekko's 280 files graff reads at a4c9c8d, 217 of them
Markdown, each question took 18 to 36 ms here, the freshness check
included, and `impact` to depth 3, over 332 callers, 83 to 86 ms (seven
runs each, 2026-10-10, on AC with TLP's performance power profile, the
CPU's boost on; its balanced profile on battery, the boost off, doubled
such times on 2026-10-09). `impact` took 521 to 535 ms before task 132:
each level asked SQL's LIKE for each name it reached, where one pass over
the sites now tells which paths go through any of them. `graff index`
runs the freshness check alone.

`graff --mcp` serves the seven questions as tools over the Model
Context Protocol, on stdin and stdout (`src/mcp.rs`), for the worktree
of the folder `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` names, as Claude Code sets it for the
servers it starts, else of the folder it was started in; a call may name
another folder, as the plugin's hook makes each call do. A tool's answer
is the command line's, cut to the `budget` the call names, at most 8,000
tokens, under the 10,000 past which Claude Code warns of a tool's output
(an estimate: graff counts 4 bytes a token); a cut that would need more
says so. It speaks both revisions ekko speaks: a request whose `_meta`
names 2026-07-28 is served on its own, `server/discover` included, and an
`initialize` handshake gets 2025-11-25 or the earlier revision it asks
for. Claude Code loads only the tools' names and the server's instructions
at a session's start, the definitions on the ToolSearch that wants them:
the instructions, 1,100 characters, say when graff answers better than
grep and when it does not, and a test holds them to 1,200 and the seven
definitions to 6,000. In one server a `def` on graff's own worktree took
18 ms a call, against 24 ms for the command line (20 calls each, three
rounds, 2026-10-12, TLP's balanced profile on battery, the load at 10 from
other sessions).

date (`src/store/history.rs`): for each commit HEAD reaches, merges aside,
the files in a language graff reads that it changed, and the definitions
its changed lines fall in, by `git diff-tree -M -U0`, each side read as
that commit has it, so a file renamed on the way is followed. A blob is
parsed once: one the index holds, as a check of the worktree leaves HEAD's,
is read from it, and the run keeps what it parsed for its other commits.
Only the commits the index lacks are mapped, and the history is kept by
repository and by the build's extractions, which say where each
definition's lines are. A definition's lines are the item's own, so a
change to its doc comment alone falls in what holds it. The commits that
touched a definition, following its file back through renames, and those
whose message holds a trailer such as `Ekko: 27`, with what they touched,
are what `Store::touching` and `Store::touched` give. On ekko at f9564f4
(359 commits, 1,502 changes to files graff reads, 1,461 blobs, 100 MB) the
whole history took 6.3 to 6.7 s, 37 s of CPU, most of it parsing; each of
its last ten commits, mapped one at a time, 69 to 482 ms, parsing nothing,
of which the worktree's check, extracting what the commit changed, takes
the most: the history alone took 50 to 83 ms (three rounds and ten
commits, 2026-10-17, TLP's performance profile on AC, the load at 17 to
25 from other sessions; `evals/history/`).

The flake's `packages.plugin` is graff's Claude Code plugin: that
server, and two hooks, `graff --hook` (`src/hook.rs`) at `SessionStart`
and before each call to one of graff's tools, all pinned to the
flake's graff by store path, so the plugin cannot run another revision
(`plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, the manifest it is made from, names
them `graff`, and a test holds every command there to that). Both hooks
take the session's folder, the `cwd` Claude Code gives hooks, before
`CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`: a session that enters a worktree moves its folder
there, while `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` and the server, which Claude Code does
not restart, stay with the checkout it started in, and a call without
`folder` was answered for that checkout (task 319, seen from inside
headless sessions of Claude Code 2.1.296). Before each call the hook puts
the session's folder in the call's `folder`, or the folder a relative
one names from it, in 9 to 24 ms, medians 11 to 12 (20 runs, two rounds,
2026-10-17, TLP's performance profile on AC, the load at 21); it runs no
git and asks nothing a call would not have asked. MCP's roots follow the
session into the worktree too, but 2026-07-28 deprecates them for a tool's
parameters, and asking for them costs each call a second round trip. At a
session's start the hook speaks only in a worktree with code in a language
graff reads: about 140 tokens (an estimate, at 4 bytes a token) naming
its files by language and the tools to ask before grep. Anywhere else,
Markdown alone included, it says nothing and costs one or two git calls:
11 to 12 ms outside a worktree, 15 to 21 ms in one of 150 to 1,900 files
(medians of 20 runs, two rounds, 2026-10-12, TLP's balanced profile, the
boost off, the load at 10 and 22). It does not index: the first question
does.

What counts as graff working was fixed before its first line of code, in
`evals/`:

- `evals/ceiling/`: what code navigation costs today, read off the transcripts.
- `evals/questions/`: 52 questions from real sessions, each with the commit it
  was asked at and the file ranges that answered it.
- `evals/bar/`: graphify and codebase-memory-mcp on those questions, the bar
  graff has to clear.
- `evals/gate/`: graff on those questions against that bar, gate A. Its
  first run failed: graff beat both over all and in every language, at fewer
  tokens, but said it found nothing on none of the questions with no answer.
  Run again by the user's leave once `search` could say nothing, it passes
  all four rules.
- `evals/verdict/`: the protocol that judges graff, and the tasks its paired
  runs will redo.

What graff does so far is measured there too:

- `evals/extract/`: the Rust extractor against a reading of its own, on ekko
  and on a cargo registry's 17,112 files.
- `evals/store/`: what keeping the index fresh costs a query, about 7 ms, and
  what a cold build costs.
- `evals/resolve/`: the edges graff draws against rust-analyzer's, on ekko and
  on graff's own source.
- `evals/query/`: the edges a question resolves for itself against those of
  the whole worktree resolved, the same for each of ekko's 3,228 definitions
  in every language it reads.
- `evals/search/`: how often `search` finds where a commit's change went,
  asked its subject, on two repositories the question set does not hold,
  and how often it finds nothing asked the other's.
- `evals/nix/`: Nix against nix's evaluation of a NixOS host (options
  declared and set, the module graph) and against nil's ties of names, on a
  NixOS flake and on nixpkgs.
- `evals/bash/`: Bash against what ran when ctx's test suite ran, traced by
  Bash itself, and against bash-language-server's ties of names, on ctx and
  on bash-completion; a function's use of its callers' locals against Bash's
  call stack as bash-completion's completions run.
- `evals/python/`: Python against pyright's ties of names, on kimi-k3-in-c's
  tools/, on ekko's and graff's evals/, and on Python 3.14's library; and
  calls against what ran when graff's evals and the library's tests ran.
- `evals/c/`: C against clangd's ties of names, on kimi-k3-in-c, with
  graphify's call edges there beside graff's, and on tree-sitter's C.
- `evals/markdown/`: Markdown against cmark-gfm, GitHub's parser, against
  the anchors GitHub gave and its rules for links, with marksman beside
  them, and its mentions of code against a model's reading of a sample,
  on ekko, ctx, kimi-k3-in-c and graff, and held out, a cargo registry's
  crates.

## Building

    nix build                  # the graff binary, in result/bin
    nix build .#plugin         # the Claude Code plugin, graff pinned in it
    nix develop                # cargo, rustc, clippy, rustfmt, rust-analyzer, python3
    cargo test
    python3 evals/bar/test_bar.py

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always

jobs:
  test:
    name: build, test & clippy
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # As in ekko's CI: v5 is the first release on Node 24.
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: clippy

      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2

      # --locked everywhere: Cargo.lock is committed, and a build that would
      # change it should fail rather than resolve other versions than a local
      # build does.
      - name: Build
        run: cargo build --locked --all-targets

      - name: Test
        run: cargo test --locked

      - name: Clippy
        run: cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings

      # The evals' own tests: the checkers and metrics gate A and gate B are
      # read with, each case holding an input that must make it say no. They
      # read no transcript and no repository of the user's.
      - name: Eval tests
        run: |
          for t in evals/*/test_*.py; do
            echo "$t"
            python3 "$t"
          done

      # Nothing else pins the declared MSRV, so it would rot while CI builds
      # on stable. Build only, as ekko's CI does.
      - name: Check the declared MSRV still builds
        run: |
          MSRV=$(grep -m1 '^rust-version' Cargo.toml | cut -d'"' -f2)
          echo "Cargo.toml declares rust-version = $MSRV"
          rustup toolchain install "$MSRV" --profile minimal
          cargo "+$MSRV" build --locked

      # The binary as a user runs it, beyond what the tests drive.
      - name: Smoke-test the binary
        run: |
          VERSION=$(grep -m1 '^version' Cargo.toml | cut -d'"' -f2)
          test "$(cargo run --locked --quiet -- --version)" = "graff $VERSION"

matters most ranked by personalized PageRank, every answer within a token
budget, from an index that re-parses
what changed on each query. Its languages are the ones used here: Rust, Nix,

host's CPython lacks a module only some platforms build (`msvcrt`, `pwd`),
or false where the name is used, an `else`'s for code in the
`if`'s block (`src/resolve/python.rs`). In C, a
file's functions, variables, structs, unions and enums (by the tag, else by
the typedef that names one), enumerators, typedefs and macros, those a
function defines for itself among them, the prototypes of what it does not
define, and the file are definitions, `static` keeping one to its file; what
only a C++ compiler reads and GCC's attributes are blanked before the parse,
each line keeping its number (`src/extract/c.rs`). `#include "x.h"` is tied
to the x.h in the including file's folder, else to the one file of the
worktree whose path ends so, with no build file read; a name to its file's
definition, else to one in what the file includes or, for a header, in what
includes it, else to the only one not `static` the linker would find, and a
prototype to the definition it declares; a definition in a branch of an
`#if` the build leaves out is none, by what the host's compiler predefines
and what the file and those it includes define, a header's include guard
among them, and the values a condition compares and computes; what a
build's flags decide stays ambiguous
(`src/resolve/c.rs`). In
Markdown, read as GitHub shows it, a file and each heading are
definitions, a heading's section running to the next heading of its level
or a higher one, named by its text and by the anchor GitHub gives it
(`src/extract/markdown.rs`). A link to a place of the worktree, a path
written in a code span or in the prose (`src/store.rs:120`), and a name a
code span writes as code names one (`Storage::load`, `k3_mmw()`,
`CTX_MIN`, not a bare `kind`) are tied to the file, the section, the
definition holding the line, or the one definition out of test code
whose full name ends as written; a Rust file stands for the `mod` items
that load it (`src/resolve/markdown.rs`). It answers seven
questions (`src/query.rs`):

    graff def Storage::load        # its lines, doc, signature, a type's impl blocks
    graff callers Storage::load    # what reaches it, by the definition each use is in
    graff callees Storage::load    # what it reaches
    graff outline src/store.rs     # what a file defines, nested, with its lines
    graff impact Storage::load     # its callers, theirs, and so on, 3 levels deep
    graff search open store        # the definitions those words find, best first
    graff map src/store.rs         # what matters most around it, by file, 1,024 tokens

A symbol is named by the end of its path (`load`, `store::Storage::load`),
with its file (`src/store.rs:Storage::load`) or by a line
(`src/store.rs:120`); a Nix file, a script, a Python module, a C file or a
Markdown one by its path (`src/lib/ledger.sh`, `k3.h`), whose callers are
what imports, sources, includes or links to it; a Rust file by its path
too, whose callers are the links and mentions of its module; and a
Markdown section by its heading, its anchor, or its file and anchor
(`Stable ids`, `stable-ids`, `readme.md#stable-ids`), by the first two only
where no code definition has the name. `def` gives a C
function's definition before its prototypes, which a budget cuts first.
`search` ranks definitions by BM25 over the words of their names, the rest
of their qualified names, their paths and their docs, an identifier split
at underscores and where its case says a word starts and kept whole too, a
word in a name counting five times, as Zoekt counts one, and test code
keeping half its score (`src/search.rs`); it gives 20 unless `--limit` says
how many. It finds nothing, rather than what shares a common word with the
question, when its best match holds too little of it: two of the
question's words, or all when it has fewer, or words that weigh by idf as
much as one only a definition alone holds, stop words aside; the answer
then names the words the best holds and those none does. `map` is Aider's repository map: the worktree's definitions
ranked by PageRank over the graph of the uses that tie them, from the
definition a use is in to the one it reaches, a use that may reach one of
several definitions weighing a tenth and one that may reach a type of std
or of Python's library none (`src/rank.rs`); each by its signature under its
file's path, the files best first, cut to 1,024 tokens unless `--budget`
says otherwise. Named files and symbols are its focus, which it leaves out:
the walk jumps to them rather than anywhere, so the map gives what they
lean on. Resolving every use of the worktree takes most of a first map,
so the graph is kept in the index, for the worktree's files and the build,
and read back by the next map until a file changes. On ekko at f9564f4
(4,799 definitions) a map took 0.09 to 0.11 s with the graph kept and
0.38 to 0.40 s making it, on kmux at 5377be7 (15,984) 0.27 s and 1.56 to
1.58 s, on Python 3.14's library (33,403) 0.41 to 0.42 s and 1.10 to
1.11 s, and on nixpkgs's nixos/modules at 71dd4e4 (116,641) 1.29 to
1.32 s and 2.43 to 2.49 s, against 0.36 to 0.38, 1.49 to 1.52, 1.04 to
1.05 and 2.37 to 2.45 s before the graph was kept, and 0.05, 0.11, 0.15
and 0.41 to 0.42 s for `outline` (five runs each, interleaved,
2026-10-12, on AC with TLP's balanced profile, the CPU's boost off, the
load at 5 to 16 from other sessions). On nixos/modules most of what is
left is writing a line for each of its definitions before the budget cuts
them. `search` does not use the graph: on the
probe of `evals/search/`, ordering its results by a walk from them, or
adding their rank to their score, did no better than BM25 alone.
An answer is cut to `--budget` tokens, 2,000 unless told, counted as 4
bytes each, least important lines first, and its last line says what it
left out and the budget that would hold it all; `--json` gives the same
answer as one object. Uses graff cannot tie to one definition, mostly
method calls on what it cannot tell the type of, are listed apart as
possible. On ekko's 280 files graff reads at a4c9c8d, 217 of them
Markdown, each question took 18 to 36 ms here, the freshness check
included, and `impact` to depth 3, over 332 callers, 83 to 86 ms (seven
runs each, 2026-10-10, on AC with TLP's performance power profile, the
CPU's boost on; its balanced profile on battery, the boost off, doubled
such times on 2026-10-09). `impact` took 521 to 535 ms before task 132:
each level asked SQL's LIKE for each name it reached, where one pass over
the sites now tells which paths go through any of them. `graff index`
runs the freshness check alone.

`graff --mcp` serves the seven questions as tools over the Model
Context Protocol, on stdin and stdout (`src/mcp.rs`), for the worktree
of the folder `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` names, as Claude Code sets it for the
servers it starts, else of the folder it was started in; a call may name
another folder, as the plugin's hook makes each call do. A tool's answer
is the command line's, cut to the `budget` the call names, at most 8,000
tokens, under the 10,000 past which Claude Code warns of a tool's output
(an estimate: graff counts 4 bytes a token); a cut that would need more
says so. It speaks both revisions ekko speaks: a request whose `_meta`
names 2026-07-28 is served on its own, `server/discover` included, and an
`initialize` handshake gets 2025-11-25 or the earlier revision it asks
for. Claude Code loads only the tools' names and the server's instructions
at a session's start, the definitions on the ToolSearch that wants them:
the instructions, 1,100 characters, say when graff answers better than
grep and when it does not, and a test holds them to 1,200 and the seven
definitions to 6,000. In one server a `def` on graff's own worktree took
18 ms a call, against 24 ms for the command line (20 calls each, three
rounds, 2026-10-12, TLP's balanced profile on battery, the load at 10 from
other sessions).

`graff history` brings the index of the repository's git history up to
date (`src/store/history.rs`): for each commit HEAD reaches, merges aside,
the files in a language graff reads that it changed, and the definitions
its changed lines fall in, by `git diff-tree -M -U0`, each side read as
that commit has it, so a file renamed on the way is followed. A blob is
parsed once: one the index holds, as a check of the worktree leaves HEAD's,
is read from it, and the run keeps what it parsed for its other commits.
Only the commits the index lacks are mapped, and the history is kept by
repository and by the build's extractions, which say where each
definition's lines are. A definition's lines are the item's own, so a
change to its doc comment alone falls in what holds it. The commits that
touched a definition, following its file back through renames, and those
whose message holds a trailer such as `Ekko: 27`, with what they touched,
are what `Store::touching` and `Store::touched` give. On ekko at f9564f4
(359 commits, 1,502 changes to files graff reads, 1,461 blobs, 100 MB) the
whole history took 6.3 to 6.7 s, 37 s of CPU, most of it parsing; each of
its last ten commits, mapped one at a time, 69 to 482 ms, parsing nothing,
of which the worktree's check, extracting what the commit changed, takes
the most: the history alone took 50 to 83 ms (three rounds and ten
commits, 2026-10-17, TLP's performance profile on AC, the load at 17 to
25 from other sessions; `evals/history/`).

The flake's `packages.plugin` is graff's Claude Code plugin: that
server, and two hooks, `graff --hook` (`src/hook.rs`) at `SessionStart`
and before each call to one of graff's tools, all pinned to the
flake's graff by store path, so the plugin cannot run another revision
(`plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, the manifest it is made from, names
them `graff`, and a test holds every command there to that). Both hooks
take the session's folder, the `cwd` Claude Code gives hooks, before
`CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`: a session that enters a worktree moves its folder
there, while `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` and the server, which Claude Code does
not restart, stay with the checkout it started in, and a call without
`folder` was answered for that checkout (task 319, seen from inside
headless sessions of Claude Code 2.1.296). Before each call the hook puts
the session's folder in the call's `folder`, or the folder a relative
one names from it, in 9 to 24 ms, medians 11 to 12 (20 runs, two rounds,
2026-10-17, TLP's performance profile on AC, the load at 21); it runs no
git and asks nothing a call would not have asked. MCP's roots follow the
session into the worktree too, but 2026-07-28 deprecates them for a tool's
parameters, and asking for them costs each call a second round trip. At a
session's start the hook speaks only in a worktree with code in a language
graff reads: about 140 tokens (an estimate, at 4 bytes a token) naming
its files by language and the tools to ask before grep. Anywhere else,
Markdown alone included, it says nothing and costs one or two git calls:
11 to 12 ms outside a worktree, 15 to 21 ms in one of 150 to 1,900 files
(medians of 20 runs, two rounds, 2026-10-12, TLP's balanced profile, the
boost off, the load at 10 and 22). It does not index: the first question
does.

What counts as graff working was fixed before its first line of code, in
`evals/`:

- `evals/ceiling/`: what code navigation costs today, read off the transcripts.
- `evals/questions/`: 52 questions from real sessions, each with the commit it
  was asked at and the file ranges that answered it.
- `evals/bar/`: graphify and codebase-memory-mcp on those questions, the bar
  graff has to clear.
- `evals/gate/`: graff on those questions against that bar, gate A. Its
  first run failed: graff beat both over all and in every language, at fewer
  tokens, but said it found nothing on none of the questions with no answer.
  Run again by the user's leave once `search` could say nothing, it passes
  all four rules.
- `evals/verdict/`: the protocol that judges graff, and the tasks its paired
  runs will redo.

What graff does so far is measured there too:

- `evals/extract/`: the Rust extractor against a reading of its own, on ekko
  and on a cargo registry's 17,112 files.
- `evals/store/`: what keeping the index fresh costs a query, about 7 ms, and
  what a cold build costs.
- `evals/resolve/`: the edges graff draws against rust-analyzer's, on ekko and
  on graff's own source.
- `evals/query/`: the edges a question resolves for itself against those of
  the whole worktree resolved, the same for each of ekko's 3,228 definitions
  in every language it reads.
- `evals/search/`: how often `search` finds where a commit's change went,
  asked its subject, on two repositories the question set does not hold,
  and how often it finds nothing asked the other's.
- `evals/nix/`: Nix against nix's evaluation of a NixOS host (options
  declared and set, the module graph) and against nil's ties of names, on a
  NixOS flake and on nixpkgs.
- `evals/bash/`: Bash against what ran when ctx's test suite ran, traced by
  Bash itself, and against bash-language-server's ties of names, on ctx and
  on bash-completion; a function's use of its callers' locals against Bash's
  call stack as bash-completion's completions run.
- `evals/python/`: Python against pyright's ties of names, on kimi-k3-in-c's
  tools/, on ekko's and graff's evals/, and on Python 3.14's library; and
  calls against what ran when graff's evals and the library's tests ran.
- `evals/c/`: C against clangd's ties of names, on kimi-k3-in-c, with
  graphify's call edges there beside graff's, and on tree-sitter's C.
- `evals/markdown/`: Markdown against cmark-gfm, GitHub's parser, against
  the anchors GitHub gave and its rules for links, with marksman beside
  them, and its mentions of code against a model's reading of a sample,
  on ekko, ctx, kimi-k3-in-c and graff, and held out, a cargo registry's
  crates.

## Building

    nix build                  # the graff binary, in result/bin
    nix build .#plugin         # the Claude Code plugin, graff pinned in it
    nix develop                # cargo, rustc, clippy, rustfmt, rust-analyzer, python3
    cargo test
    python3 evals/bar/test_bar.py

## License

MIT, in `LICENSE`.
